items.question: How do a set and a frozenset differ in Python, and when would you reach for the frozen one?
items.answer: Both are unordered collections of unique, hashable items with fast membership tests. A set is mutable, so you can add and remove items, but that also makes it unhashable. A frozenset is immutable and hashable, so it can be a dictionary key or live inside another set, which is handy for caching on a group of tags or deduplicating combinations.
keyPoints: Both give O(1) average membership checks
Use frozenset as a dict key or inside another set

items.question: Explain shallow versus deep copy, and why two variables holding the same small integer can report the same id().
items.answer: A shallow copy builds a new outer container but reuses references to the inner objects, so mutating a nested list shows up in both copies. A deep copy recursively copies nested objects so the two are independent. Separately, CPython caches small integers (roughly -5 to 256) and some strings, so separate assignments of the same small value point at one object and id() matches; this is an implementation detail, so compare values with == and not with is.
keyPoints: CPython interns small ints, so ids can match
Use == for values, is only for identity such as None

items.question: Why does equivalent code usually run faster in C than in Python? Walk through what happens when Python runs a script.
items.answer: C is compiled ahead of time to machine code with static types, so the CPU runs tight instructions directly. CPython compiles source to bytecode and then interprets it in a loop, and every operation does dynamic type checks, reference counting and boxed-object lookups. That overhead is why heavy numeric work is pushed into C-backed libraries like NumPy or into vectorised calls.
keyPoints: Python: source to bytecode, then the interpreter loop
Dynamic typing and boxed objects add per-operation cost
Push hot loops into C-backed libraries

items.question: Reverse the order of words in a sentence without using built-in helpers like split or reversed.
items.answer: Walk the string once, collecting characters into the current word and pushing finished words onto a list when you hit a space. Then build the output by reading that list from the end, inserting single spaces. It is O(n) time and O(n) space; mention how you treat repeated or leading spaces before you start coding.
keyPoints: Single pass to tokenise on spaces
Rebuild from the last word to the first
Clarify handling of extra whitespace up front

items.question: What does __init__ do in a Python class, why the double underscores, and what does a single leading underscore on a method signal?
items.answer: __init__ initialises a new instance after it is created, setting up its attributes. Double underscores on both sides mark special methods that Python calls for you (dunder methods), so they do not clash with your own names. A single leading underscore is a convention meaning internal or private by agreement; Python does not enforce it, while a double leading underscore without trailing ones triggers name mangling.
keyPoints: __init__ initialises, it does not construct (that is __new__)
Dunder names are hooks the interpreter calls

items.question: What is abstraction in Python OOP? Sketch a short inheritance example.
items.answer: Abstraction exposes what an object does while hiding how. In Python you often express it with an abstract base class from abc whose abstract methods subclasses must implement. For example, a base LLMClient with an abstract complete(prompt) method, and OpenAIClient and LocalClient subclasses that each implement it, lets the rest of the code depend only on the base type.
keyPoints: Abstraction hides implementation behind an interface
Callers depend on the base type, not concrete classes

items.question: Write Python that reads a CSV and fills missing values in numeric columns with each column's median.
items.answer: With pandas: read the file with read_csv, select numeric columns, compute their medians and call fillna with that mapping. items.question: How do you handle missing data in pandas?
items.answer: First measure it with isna().sum() and understand why values are missing. Then choose per column: drop rows or columns when missingness is rare or useless, impute with mean, median, mode or a forward fill for time series, or add an indicator column so a model can learn from the fact that a value was missing. Validate that the choice does not distort the distribution you care about.
keyPoints: Drop, impute or flag, chosen per column

items.question: Build an iterator class, extend it to walk a 2D structure, then turn it into an async iterator.
items.answer: Start with __iter__ and __next__ holding explicit position state and raising StopIteration at the end. For 2D, keep a row and column index and skip empty rows. For async, implement __aiter__ and an async __anext__ that awaits the data source and raises StopAsyncIteration; callers then use async for. Talk through how state survives between calls and what happens on empty input.
keyPoints: 2D: row and column cursors, skip empty rows
__aiter__ and async __anext__ for the async version

items.question: Write an iterator that lazily flattens an arbitrarily nested list of lists and integers, using explicit state and no generators.
items.answer: Keep a stack of (list, index) frames. In __next__, look at the top frame: if its index is past the end, pop it; if the next element is a list, advance the index and push a new frame for that list; if it is an integer, advance and return it. Raise StopIteration when the stack is empty. This handles arbitrary depth without recursion limits.
keyPoints: Push on nested list, pop when exhausted
Return integers as they are reached
No recursion, so depth is not limited

items.question: Implement encode and decode for a list of strings so that any string content, including delimiters, round-trips exactly.
items.answer: Use length-prefixing: for each string write its length, a separator such as '#', then the raw string. Decoding reads digits up to the separator, then slices exactly that many characters. Unlike a plain delimiter join, this survives strings that contain the delimiter or are empty.
keyPoints: Length prefix plus separator per item
Decode by reading the length, then slicing
Handles empty strings and embedded delimiters
Escaping is the alternative, but is easier to get wrong

items.question: Given a helper that fetches one URL, write a crawler that covers a domain, first synchronously and then concurrently.
items.answer: Synchronous version: a BFS queue of URLs, a visited set, and a filter that keeps only links on the same host. For the concurrent version, use asyncio with a bounded number of workers (a semaphore or fixed worker tasks pulling from an asyncio.Queue), mark URLs visited when enqueued to avoid duplicate work, and handle timeouts. Interviewers follow up on politeness, deduplication and how you know you are done.
keyPoints: BFS with a visited set and same-host filter
Bounded concurrency with workers and a queue
Mark visited on enqueue, not on fetch
Timeouts, politeness and a clean stop condition

items.question: Implement a thread-safe batching logger: many threads call log(msg), and a background thread flushes up to 100 messages at a time, every second or as soon as a batch is full.
items.answer: Protect a shared buffer with a lock and a condition variable. log() appends and notifies when the buffer reaches 100. The flusher waits on the condition with a one second timeout, swaps the buffer for an empty one while holding the lock, then writes outside the lock. Add a close() that sets a flag, wakes the flusher and drains what is left.
keyPoints: Lock plus condition variable around the buffer
Wake on full batch or one second timeout
Swap buffers under the lock, write outside it

items.question: Design an object-oriented system for courses, students and grades.
items.answer: Model Student, Course and Enrollment (or Grade) as separate classes, with the enrollment linking a student to a course and holding the grade. Keep behaviour where the data lives, such as Course.average() and Student.gpa(). Type-hint everything, validate grade ranges, and expect the interviewer to add requirements, so keep classes small and avoid hard-coding assumptions.

Behaviour lives next to its data
Small classes that absorb new requirements

items.question: You get about 120 lines of messy code that works and has passing tests. Improve the design without breaking anything. What do you change first?
items.answer: Run the tests first so you know the baseline, then read for the worst readability problem: usually deep nesting or one function doing many jobs. Make small, behaviour-preserving moves (extract function, early returns, clearer names), rerunning tests after each. Explain why each change helps the next requirement, and do not reach for a big rewrite.

Justify changes by what they make easier next

items.question: A function tallies values into a dictionary and double counts some keys. Find and fix the bug.
items.answer: Reproduce with the smallest input that double counts, then trace where a key gets incremented. Typical causes are incrementing in two branches, iterating over a structure while also adding to it, or a missing else. Fix it, then add a regression test for the failing input before moving on.

Trace every place the key is incremented
Look for duplicate branches and mutation during iteration

items.question: Write a function that returns the first n Fibonacci numbers.
items.answer: Iterate with two running values instead of recursion, appending to a list until it holds n items. Handle n = 0 and n = 1 explicitly and mention that naive recursion is exponential. A generator version is a nice extension when n is large or unknown.

items.question: Write a function that computes root-mean-square error from two lists of predictions and targets.
items.answer: Check the lists are the same non-zero length, sum the squared differences, divide by n and take the square root. Mention a NumPy one-liner, and that RMSE weights large errors heavily compared with MAE.

items.question: Implement an LRU cache with O(1) get and put, then add a time-to-live per entry.
items.answer: Combine a hash map from key to node with a doubly linked list ordered by recency. get moves the node to the front; put inserts at the front and evicts from the tail when over capacity. In Python, OrderedDict with move_to_end gives the same behaviour. For TTL, store an expiry time on each entry and treat expired entries as misses, deleting them lazily on access.
keyPoints: Hash map plus doubly linked list
Move to front on access, evict the tail
TTL: store expiry, expire lazily on read

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Given a stream of user actions, return the k items with the most engagement. Then explain why a heap might be the wrong choice in production.
items.answer: Count per item in a hash map and keep a min-heap of size k for the current top k, which is O(n log k). In production the stream is unbounded and spread across machines, so exact counts per item do not fit in memory and heaps do not merge cheaply. You would use approximate sketches such as Count-Min with a heavy-hitters structure, windowed counts, and periodic merges.
keyPoints: Hash map counts plus size-k min-heap
O(n log k) for a bounded stream
Unbounded, distributed streams break exact counting
Count-Min sketch or heavy hitters, merged per window

items.question: Convert nested stack trace samples into a flat list of function start and end events.
items.answer: Treat each sample as the current call stack. Compare it with the previous sample: frames that disappeared emit end events (innermost first), and new frames emit start events (outermost first). Watch for recursion, where the same function name appears twice, so compare by position in the stack and not just by name.
keyPoints: Ends for popped frames, innermost first
Starts for new frames, outermost first
Compare by stack position to handle recursion

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Build an in-memory database in stages: set, get and delete; then filtered scans; then per-key TTL; then compaction to a file.
items.answer: Start with a dict of key to record. Scans iterate keys and apply a predicate, optionally keeping a sorted index for prefix scans. TTL adds an expiry timestamp, and reads take the current time as a parameter so tests are deterministic. Compaction writes only live, unexpired entries to a new file and atomically swaps it in. The point of the exercise is keeping the design clean as levels stack up.
keyPoints: Dict-backed core with clear method boundaries
Scans with a predicate or sorted index
Pass timestamps in for deterministic TTL
Compaction writes live entries and swaps atomically

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Implement an in-memory key-value store with set, get, and transactions that support begin, commit and abort.
items.answer: Keep a base dict plus a stack of transaction layers. Writes go to the top layer, with a tombstone marker for deletes; reads check layers from the top down, then the base. Commit merges the top layer into the one below (or the base), and abort just pops it. Discuss the cost of reads with deep stacks and what isolation you are promising.
keyPoints: Stack of change layers over a base dict

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Extend a key-value store with BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK where transactions can be nested.
items.answer: Use one layer per open transaction on a stack. ROLLBACK discards only the innermost layer, COMMIT folds the innermost into its parent so the outer transaction can still roll it back, and the outermost commit writes to the base. Define what COMMIT means with no open transaction and test interleaved set, delete and rollback sequences.
keyPoints: Inner commit merges into the parent, not the base
Rollback drops only the innermost layer
Define behaviour with no open transaction

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Implement a task scheduler that runs jobs at given times.
items.answer: Keep a min-heap keyed by next run time. A loop pops due tasks, runs them (on a worker pool if they may block) and re-schedules recurring ones. Make the clock injectable for testing, decide what happens to tasks that overrun, and add cancellation by marking entries as cancelled rather than searching the heap.
keyPoints: Min-heap ordered by next run time

items.question: What are Python's built-in data structures, and how do arrays differ from strings?
items.answer: The core ones are list (mutable, ordered), tuple (immutable, ordered), dict (key to value) and set (unique items). Strings are immutable sequences of characters, so every change creates a new string, whereas a list or array.array can be modified in place. Arrays from the array module or NumPy also store one element type compactly.
keyPoints: list, tuple, dict, set and their mutability
Arrays store one type compactly and are mutable

items.question: Find duplicate files across a large file system.
items.answer: Group by file size first since only same-size files can match. Within a size group, hash a small prefix to cut candidates, then compute a full content hash (for example SHA-256) and group by it. Stream file contents in chunks so memory stays flat, and consider a final byte comparison if collisions matter.
keyPoints: Cheap prefix hash, then full hash

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: List the main REST methods and explain the difference between PUT and PATCH.
items.answer: GET reads, POST creates or triggers an action, PUT replaces a resource, PATCH updates part of it and DELETE removes it. PUT sends the full representation and is idempotent: sending it twice leaves the same state. PATCH sends only the changed fields and is not guaranteed to be idempotent, for example an append operation.
keyPoints: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE roles
PUT is idempotent, PATCH may not be

source.title: Accenture LLM Operations Engineer interview experience (GeeksforGeeks)

items.question: What happens between typing a site's URL into a browser and seeing the page?
items.answer: The browser parses the URL, checks caches, and resolves the host through DNS. It opens a TCP connection (and TLS handshake for HTTPS), sends the HTTP request, and the request passes through load balancers or gateways to an application server, which may call databases and services. The response comes back with a status, headers and body, and the browser parses HTML and fetches CSS, JS and images before rendering.
keyPoints: Load balancer, app server, data stores

source.title: Fynd Junior Python Engineer interview experience (GeeksforGeeks)

items.question: What is the TCP three-way handshake?
items.answer: Before data flows, the client sends SYN with its initial sequence number, the server replies SYN-ACK acknowledging it and sending its own, and the client sends ACK. Both sides now agree on sequence numbers so TCP can deliver bytes reliably and in order. It costs one round trip before the first request, which is why connection reuse and keep-alive matter for latency.
keyPoints: Costs a round trip, so reuse connections

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: Explain a cross-site scripting (XSS) attack and how to prevent it.
items.answer: XSS happens when an attacker gets their script to run in another user's browser on your site, for example by storing a comment containing a script tag that is rendered unescaped. The script can then read the page, act as the user or steal cookies that are not HttpOnly. Prevent it by escaping output for its context, using templating that escapes by default, a Content Security Policy, and HttpOnly cookies.
keyPoints: Injected script runs in a victim's browser
CSP and HttpOnly cookies limit damage

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: Design a payment-processing service. The interviewer pushes on retries, idempotency and failure recovery.
items.answer: Clients send an idempotency key with each charge request; the server stores the key with the request's result so a retry returns the same outcome instead of charging twice. Use a state machine per payment (created, authorised, captured, failed), write state changes durably before calling the payment provider, and reconcile with the provider for requests whose outcome is unknown after a timeout. Retries use backoff and only on safe failures.
keyPoints: Idempotency keys stored with the result

source.title: OpenAI software engineer interview guide (Aced, formerly Exponent)

items.question: Design a webhook delivery system that reliably delivers events to URLs your customers register.
items.answer: Persist each event, then enqueue a delivery job per subscribed endpoint. Workers POST with a signature header, treat 2xx as success, and retry other results with exponential backoff and jitter up to a limit, then park the delivery in a dead-letter state the customer can replay. Deliveries are at-least-once, so include an event id for receivers to deduplicate, and isolate slow endpoints so they cannot block others.
keyPoints: Durable event log and per-endpoint queue
Backoff retries then dead letter with replay
At-least-once with event ids for dedup

items.question: Write a function that pulls every record from a paginated REST API.
items.answer: Loop: request a page, collect its items, and follow the cursor or next link (or compute the next page number from page size and total) until there are no more. Handle rate limits and transient errors with retries, and avoid off-by-one errors when the total is an exact multiple of the page size. For very large sets, yield pages instead of building one huge list.
keyPoints: Follow cursor or next link until done
Yield pages to keep memory flat

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Take-home task: build a movies API with genres, rating, director and cast, in the framework of your choice.
items.answer: Model movies, people and genres with many-to-many links, expose list, detail, create and update endpoints with filtering by genre and rating, and validate input with response and request models. Add pagination, a few tests, and a README with run instructions. Packaging it in Docker and deploying it is a strong extra.
keyPoints: Clean data model with many-to-many links
Tests, README and an easy way to run it

source.title: Fynd Junior Python Engineer interview experience (GeeksforGeeks)

items.question: Walk through the path of an HTTP request through a Python web framework during an API call.
items.answer: The web server (for example uvicorn or gunicorn) accepts the connection and hands the request to the app. Middleware runs first (logging, auth, CORS), then the router matches the path and method to a handler, parameters are parsed and validated, dependencies are resolved, and the handler runs business logic and database calls. The response travels back out through middleware, which can add headers, before it is sent.
keyPoints: Server to app interface (ASGI or WSGI)

source.title: Fynd Junior Python Engineer interview experience (GeeksforGeeks)

items.question: Pair programming: build a service that takes a user question, enriches it with data from a third-party API, and answers using a chat model API. How do you structure it?
items.answer: Split it into a thin HTTP handler, a client for the third-party API, a client for the model, and an orchestration function between them. Use async HTTP calls with timeouts, run independent calls concurrently, and decide what to do when enrichment fails (answer without it and say so). Keep prompts in one place, type the data passed between steps, and write tests with fake clients.
keyPoints: Typed boundaries and tests with fakes

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Compare relational databases with NoSQL stores. When would you choose each?
items.answer: Relational databases give a fixed schema, joins, constraints and ACID transactions, which suits data with strong relationships and correctness needs like orders or payments. NoSQL covers document, key-value, wide-column and graph stores that trade some of that for flexible schemas, horizontal scale or specific access patterns. Choose from your query patterns and consistency needs, and remember Postgres with JSON columns covers many 'flexible' cases.
keyPoints: Decide from access patterns and consistency
Postgres JSON covers many hybrid needs

source.title: Fynd Junior Python Engineer interview experience (GeeksforGeeks)

items.question: Would adding an index to every column make queries faster or slower?
items.answer: Reads on those columns may get faster, but every insert, update and delete now has to maintain every index, so writes slow down and storage grows. The planner also only uses indexes that match the query's filters and sort order. Index the columns your real queries filter, join and sort on, use composite indexes in the right column order, and check with EXPLAIN.
keyPoints: Each index slows writes and uses space

source.title: Fynd Junior Python Engineer interview experience (GeeksforGeeks)

items.question: Design the schema for a many-to-many relationship, such as processes and recipes, and write the query that fetches one side with its related items.
items.answer: Create the two entity tables and a join table holding both foreign keys (plus any relationship attributes), with a composite primary key or unique constraint. Query with a JOIN through the join table, filtering by the entity you start from. Mention indexing both foreign keys and how an ORM expresses the same thing.
keyPoints: Two entity tables plus a join table

source.title: Fynd Junior Python Engineer interview experience (GeeksforGeeks)

items.question: Write SQL to find the five pairs of products most often bought together.
items.answer: Self-join the order items table on order id with a.product_id < b.product_id so each pair appears once and a product never pairs with itself. Group by the pair, count distinct orders, order by that count descending and limit 5. Mention the cost of the self-join on big tables and filtering to recent orders first.
keyPoints: Filter early to control join size

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Write SQL that detects whether any user has overlapping subscription date ranges.
items.answer: Self-join subscriptions on user id with a.id < b.id and the overlap condition a.start_date <= b.end_date and b.start_date <= a.end_date. Alternatively use a window function: order each user's rows by start date and compare each start with the previous row's end using LAG. Clarify whether touching endpoints count and how open-ended subscriptions (null end) are treated.
keyPoints: Overlap test: a.start <= b.end and b.start <= a.end
Self-join or LAG over ordered rows
Avoid comparing a row with itself
Define inclusive ends and null end dates

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: An ETL bug inserted a new salary row for every employee every year instead of updating. Return each employee's current salary.
items.answer: Rank each employee's rows with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id ORDER BY effective_date DESC, id DESC) and keep row 1. If there is no reliable date, the highest surrogate id per employee is the latest insert. Mention a tie-breaker and how you would fix the data upstream.
keyPoints: Tie-break on id when dates match
Fix the ETL as well as the query

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Using Python and SQLite, find employees with more than three leave requests in the previous month.
items.answer: Connect with sqlite3, then run a parameterised query that filters leave requests to the previous calendar month, groups by employee id and keeps groups with HAVING COUNT(*) > 3, joining employees for names. Compute the month boundaries in Python or with SQLite date functions, and never build the SQL with string formatting.
keyPoints: Filter by date range for last month
GROUP BY employee with HAVING COUNT(*) > 3

source.title: Accenture LLM Operations Engineer interview experience (GeeksforGeeks)

items.question: Write a SQL query that joins and aggregates several tables to answer a business question.
items.answer: Restate the question as the grain of the output (one row per what?), pick the tables and join keys, choose inner or left joins deliberately, then aggregate with GROUP BY and filter groups with HAVING. Watch for row multiplication when joining one-to-many tables before aggregating; aggregate in a subquery or CTE first if needed.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: You have customer exports from three systems with overlapping records. Produce one deduplicated set of customer entities and explain the design.
items.answer: Normalise fields (case, whitespace, phone and email formats), then block candidates on cheap keys like email domain or postcode so you only compare plausible pairs. Score pairs with exact and fuzzy matches, link matches into clusters with union-find, and pick a surviving value per field with clear precedence rules. Keep the source ids on each entity for traceability and send low-confidence matches for review.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Build a small ORM step by step.
items.answer: Start with a base Model class whose subclasses declare fields; a metaclass or __init_subclass__ collects them into a table definition. Add save() that generates parameterised INSERT or UPDATE statements and a query API that builds SELECTs with filters. Map rows back to objects, then extend with relationships and transactions if time allows.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What is the difference between rebasing and squashing in git?
items.answer: Rebase replays your commits on top of another base, giving a linear history without a merge commit; each commit is kept but rewritten. Squash combines several commits into one, either with interactive rebase or a squash merge, so a feature lands as a single commit. Both rewrite history, so avoid them on branches other people have pulled.
keyPoints: Rebase moves commits onto a new base

source.title: IBM Associate Software Developer interview experience (Taro)

items.question: Explain git merge versus git rebase, and when you would use each.
items.answer: Merge joins two histories with a merge commit and preserves exactly what happened, which is safe for shared branches. Rebase rewrites your commits on top of the target for a linear history, which is nice for updating a private feature branch before review. A common team rule is rebase locally, merge (or squash-merge) into main.
keyPoints: Merge preserves history with a merge commit
Rebase gives a linear history by rewriting

source.title: Git interview questions (GeeksforGeeks)

items.question: What is a merge conflict and how do you resolve one?
items.answer: A conflict happens when both sides changed the same lines (or one deleted a file the other edited) and git cannot pick automatically. Open the conflicted files, decide the correct combined code between the markers, remove the markers, run the tests, then git add and continue the merge or rebase. Small, frequent merges keep conflicts small.
keyPoints: Both sides edited the same region
Edit between markers, then remove them
Test before git add and continue
Integrate often to keep conflicts small

source.title: Git interview questions (GeeksforGeeks)

items.question: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull, and between reset and revert?
items.answer: fetch downloads new commits from the remote without changing your branch; pull is fetch followed by merge (or rebase). reset moves your branch pointer back and can discard commits, which rewrites history; revert adds a new commit that undoes an earlier one, which is safe on shared branches.
keyPoints: revert undoes with a new commit

source.title: Git interview questions (GeeksforGeeks)

items.question: A community contributor opens a pull request adding a new model architecture to a popular open-source library. You are the reviewing maintainer: what do you check, and how do you handle the interaction?
items.answer: Check that it follows the library's conventions, that outputs match the reference implementation numerically, that tests and docs are included, and that it does not slow or break shared code paths. Run CI and try it yourself. Be specific and kind in comments, separate blocking issues from nits, and offer to help with the hard parts so the contributor stays engaged.
keyPoints: Conventions and parity with the reference implementation
Clear, respectful feedback; blockers versus nits

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Given two snapshots of a repository (path to content), build a Merkle tree and return which files changed without comparing every file.
items.answer: Hash each file's content, then hash each directory from its children's names and hashes, up to a root. Compare the two roots: if equal, nothing changed. Otherwise recurse only into children whose hashes differ, which skips unchanged subtrees entirely. This is the same idea git uses for trees, and it makes sync and re-indexing cheap.
keyPoints: File hash from content, directory hash from children
Same idea as git tree objects

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design a hub that hosts millions of git repositories where single files can be tens or hundreds of gigabytes.
items.answer: Keep git for metadata and small files, and store large files in object storage addressed by content hash, with pointer files in git (the LFS approach, or chunk-level deduplication). Serve downloads through a CDN with range requests and resumable uploads, deduplicate identical chunks across repos, and separate the metadata database from blob storage so each scales independently.
keyPoints: Git for metadata, object storage for big blobs

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: You are dropped into an unfamiliar multi-file codebase with a failing behaviour and an LLM assistant available. Walk through how you fix it.
items.answer: Reproduce the failure first and get a fast loop for running it. Use the assistant to map the code (entry points, the path the failing request takes), but confirm what it says by reading the code. Form a hypothesis, add a failing test or log line, make the smallest fix, and verify with the tests. Narrate where you trust the tool and where you check it.
keyPoints: Reproduce and get a fast feedback loop
Use the assistant to explore, then verify

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: A scheduler class in a small LLM inference engine has one stub method with no spec, docstring or tests. Walk through your first thirty minutes.
items.answer: Read how the method is called and what state the class keeps, so you can infer the contract: which requests get admitted, under which memory or batch limits. Write that contract down as a short spec and confirm it with the interviewer, then write tests for the obvious cases and edge cases before implementing. Keep the first version simple and correct.
keyPoints: Infer the contract from callers and state
Write a mini spec and confirm assumptions

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Some loops include a round where you are given an AI assistant and graded on how you direct and verify it. How do you show good judgement in that round?
items.answer: Give the assistant clear, scoped tasks with the relevant context, review every diff instead of accepting it wholesale, and run tests or small checks after each change. Say out loud when you disagree with its output and why. The signal they want is that you stay in charge of correctness and design while using the tool for speed.
keyPoints: Scoped prompts with the right context
Verify with tests after each step

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How would you use AI to improve the test coverage and reliability of a service?
items.answer: Use coverage reports to find untested paths, then have an assistant draft unit and property tests for them, reviewing that they assert real behaviour and not the current bugs. Generate edge-case inputs and fuzz cases, summarise flaky tests from CI history, and add AI review on pull requests. Measure the effect with coverage, escaped defects and flake rate.

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: How do you use AI in your day-to-day work?
items.answer: Give concrete examples: exploring an unfamiliar codebase, drafting tests, writing boilerplate, reviewing diffs, or summarising documents, plus where you deliberately do not use it. Mention how you verify output and one time it saved real time and one time it was wrong. Interviewers want judgement, not enthusiasm.
keyPoints: A win and a failure story

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: Describe how you have adopted AI in your workflows, with examples.
items.answer: Pick two or three workflows, explain what you did before, what you changed, and the measured effect (time saved, quality, fewer errors). Include how you rolled it out to a team, if you did, and what guardrails you added. Close with what you would try next.
keyPoints: Before and after for each workflow

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: In a build session you get two hours and any AI tools you like. How do you decide what to build and spend the time?
items.answer: Spend the first minutes scoping a small, demoable slice and writing a short plan with acceptance checks. Use AI tools to move fast on scaffolding while keeping the core logic understood. Leave time to test the main path, handle one failure case and prepare a short demo explaining trade-offs and what you would do next.
keyPoints: AI for speed, you for core logic
Reserve time to test and demo

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: You have four hours to build and demo a working AI-powered product. How do you spend them?
items.answer: Choose one user and one job to be done, then aim for a working end-to-end path in the first hour or so, even if crude. Improve the parts the demo depends on, add basic error handling and a fallback when the model misbehaves, and stop building with time left to rehearse. Explain what you cut and why.
keyPoints: Stop early to rehearse; explain cuts

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?
items.answer: An image is a read-only template made of layers: the filesystem plus metadata such as the start command. A container is a running (or stopped) instance of an image with its own writable layer, process and network namespace. Many containers can run from one image.
keyPoints: Container: running instance with a writable layer
Containers are disposable, images are versioned

source.title: Docker interview questions (GeeksforGeeks)

items.question: How do containers differ from virtual machines?
items.answer: A VM virtualises hardware and runs a full guest OS on a hypervisor, so it is heavier and slower to start but strongly isolated. Containers share the host kernel and isolate processes with namespaces and cgroups, so they start in seconds and are lighter, with weaker isolation. Many platforms run containers inside VMs to get both.
keyPoints: VM: guest OS on a hypervisor
Container: shared kernel, namespaces and cgroups
Containers are lighter and faster to start

source.title: Docker interview questions (GeeksforGeeks)

items.question: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT in a Dockerfile?
items.answer: ENTRYPOINT sets the executable that always runs; CMD supplies default arguments (or a default command if there is no ENTRYPOINT) that are replaced by whatever you pass to docker run. A common pattern is ENTRYPOINT for the program and CMD for default flags. Use the exec (JSON array) form so signals reach your process.
keyPoints: Combine them for program plus default args

source.title: Docker interview questions (GeeksforGeeks)

items.question: How do you make a Docker image smaller and faster to build?
items.answer: Start from a slim base image, use multi-stage builds so compilers and build tools stay out of the final image, and order instructions so rarely changing layers (dependency install) come before frequently changing ones (copying source) to reuse the cache. Add a .dockerignore, combine and clean up package installs in the same layer, and do not bake secrets into layers.

source.title: Docker interview questions (GeeksforGeeks)

items.question: Monolith or microservices: how do you compare them and when would you pick each?
items.answer: A monolith is one deployable unit: simple to build, test and debug, with in-process calls and one database, but it scales and deploys as a whole. Microservices split the system into independently deployable services that can scale and evolve separately, at the cost of network calls, distributed failures, data consistency work and heavier operations. Start with a well-structured monolith and split out services when team size or scaling needs justify it.
keyPoints: Monolith: simple, one deploy, shared database
Split when a clear need appears

source.title: Fynd Junior Python Engineer interview experience (GeeksforGeeks)

items.question: You inherit an 800-line pipeline script from a previous deployment. It is slow and sometimes produces wrong numbers, and the author has left. What do you do?
items.answer: First capture current behaviour: run it on a known input and save outputs as a baseline, and find a case where the numbers are wrong. Profile to find where time goes. Break the script into stages with clear inputs and outputs, add assertions and tests around the stage that produces wrong numbers (often joins that fan out, timezone or dedup bugs), fix it, then optimise the slow stage. Document what you learned for the next person.
keyPoints: Freeze a baseline before changing anything
Fix correctness before speed, then document

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Explain the fundamentals behind transformers and large language models.
items.answer: An LLM is a transformer trained to predict the next token over a huge text corpus. Text is tokenised, tokens become embeddings, and stacked blocks of self-attention and feed-forward layers let each position use information from earlier positions. After pretraining, instruction tuning and preference tuning shape it into a helpful assistant, and at inference it generates one token at a time.

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: What are the risks of assuming an LLM thinks or feels like a human?
items.answer: People over-trust fluent text, assume the model has stable beliefs, memory or intent, and read confidence as knowledge. That leads to skipped verification, emotional reliance, and wrong mental models of failures (the model is not 'lying', it is generating likely text). Design products and evaluations around measured behaviour, make limits visible, and avoid UX that encourages attachment.
keyPoints: No guaranteed beliefs, memory or intent
Misread failures lead to wrong fixes
Design and evaluate on measured behaviour

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: What do the Chinchilla scaling laws say, and how did they change earlier intuitions about scaling?
items.answer: Earlier scaling work suggested putting most extra compute into bigger models. Chinchilla found that for a fixed compute budget, loss is minimised by scaling parameters and training tokens roughly equally, about 20 tokens per parameter, so many large models were undertrained. In practice teams now often train smaller models on far more data than 'compute optimal' because inference cost matters too.
keyPoints: Fixed compute: grow data and parameters together
Inference cost pushes toward smaller, longer-trained models

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How does byte pair encoding work, and where does it fail (numbers, code, non-Latin scripts)?
items.answer: BPE starts from characters or bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token until it reaches the vocabulary size. Common words become single tokens while rare ones split into pieces. It struggles with numbers (inconsistent digit splits hurt arithmetic), code whitespace, and languages under-represented in the training corpus, which get split into many more tokens and so cost more and fit less in context.
keyPoints: Merge most frequent pairs until vocab size
Under-represented scripts get many more tokens

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Write code to measure a tokenizer's fertility across languages, and say what you would do with the result.
items.answer: Fertility is tokens per word (or per character) on a parallel corpus. Load the tokenizer, encode the same sentences in each language, and divide token counts by word counts. High fertility means higher cost, slower generation and less effective context for that language; fixes are extending the vocabulary with tokens for that script, training a new tokenizer, or choosing a model whose tokenizer is better balanced.
keyPoints: Tokens per word on parallel text
High fertility raises cost and latency
Extend vocab or pick a better tokenizer

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Why is tokenization the first bottleneck for Indian-language LLMs, and how does a low-fertility tokenizer change the economics?
items.answer: Tokenizers trained mostly on English split Indic scripts into many tokens per word, so the same sentence costs several times more tokens. That multiplies API cost, slows generation, and fills the context window faster. A tokenizer with good coverage of those scripts cuts tokens per word, which directly lowers cost per request and latency and lets more content fit in context.
keyPoints: More tokens means more cost and latency

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Compare BPE, WordPiece and Unigram tokenization. Why are fast tokenizers written in Rust, and what tokenizer bugs bite people in practice?
items.answer: BPE merges frequent pairs; WordPiece picks merges that most increase likelihood and marks word pieces; Unigram starts with a big vocabulary and prunes it, choosing the most likely segmentation. Rust implementations make tokenising large datasets fast and allow parallelism. Common bugs: mismatched tokenizer and model versions, missing or duplicated special tokens like BOS, whitespace handling differences, and wrong padding side for generation.
keyPoints: Bugs: version mismatch, special tokens, whitespace, padding side

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: A model family uses byte-level BPE with roughly 151K tokens, extra multilingual coverage, and digits split into single characters. Why those choices, and what do they trade off?
items.answer: Byte-level BPE means any input can be encoded with no unknown tokens. A large vocabulary lowers token counts for many languages and code, at the cost of a bigger embedding and output layer. Splitting digits one per token makes arithmetic consistent because numbers are always tokenised the same way, although numbers then take more tokens.
keyPoints: Big vocab: fewer tokens, bigger embedding matrix

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What changes in tokenization, data and evaluation when one model must serve both Chinese and English well?
items.answer: The tokenizer needs good coverage of Chinese characters and common words as well as English subwords, or one language becomes far more expensive. Training data must be balanced so neither language degrades, with care for quality in both. Evaluation needs native benchmarks in each language, not just translations, plus checks for code-switching inputs.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Explain scaled dot-product attention and why it divides by the square root of the key dimension.
items.answer: Each position forms a query and compares it with every key by dot product; a softmax over those scores gives weights used to average the values. Dot products of d-dimensional vectors grow in variance with d, which pushes softmax into saturated regions with tiny gradients. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) keeps the scores at unit scale so training stays stable.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Implement scaled dot-product attention with a causal mask from scratch.
items.answer: Compute scores = Q @ K.T / sqrt(d_k), add a mask that sets positions above the diagonal to negative infinity so a token cannot see the future, apply a numerically stable softmax (subtract the row max), and multiply by V. Check shapes for batch and heads, and mention that fused kernels do the same in one pass.
keyPoints: Scores from Q and K, scaled
Weighted sum of V, check shapes

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Implement multi-head attention, then convert it to grouped-query attention.
items.answer: Project inputs to Q, K and V, reshape into heads, run attention per head and concatenate before an output projection. For GQA, keep the same number of query heads but fewer K and V heads, and repeat each K/V head across its group of query heads. This shrinks the KV cache by the group factor with little quality loss.
keyPoints: Project, split heads, attend, concat, project
GQA: fewer K and V heads
Repeat each K/V head across its query group
KV cache shrinks by the group size

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What are multi-query attention and grouped-query attention, and what do they give up?
items.answer: MQA shares one key and value head across all query heads; GQA shares each K/V head across a group of query heads. Both shrink the KV cache and memory bandwidth during decoding, which raises throughput and allows longer contexts. They trade a little model quality and expressiveness, with GQA as the middle ground most modern models use.
keyPoints: MQA: one K/V head for all queries
GQA: one K/V head per group
Smaller KV cache and faster decode
Slight quality cost; GQA is the compromise

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What is multi-head latent attention and why was it introduced?
items.answer: MLA compresses keys and values into a small shared latent vector per token and caches that instead of full per-head K and V, reconstructing them with learned up-projections when needed. This cuts KV cache memory far more than GQA while keeping per-head expressiveness. Positional information needs special handling (a separate rotary component) because the compression does not commute with RoPE.
keyPoints: Cache a low-rank latent instead of full K/V

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What is a mixture-of-experts model, and how does it add capacity without adding as many FLOPs?
items.answer: The feed-forward layer is replaced by many expert networks and a router that sends each token to only a few of them (top-k). Total parameters grow with the number of experts, but compute per token depends only on the experts used. The costs are memory to hold all experts, load-balancing problems, and communication when experts live on different devices.
keyPoints: Many expert FFNs plus a router
Each token uses only k experts
Parameters grow, per-token FLOPs do not

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Why does a sparse MoE with about 47B total parameters run at roughly the cost of a 13B dense model?
items.answer: With eight experts and two chosen per token, each token passes through the shared layers plus two experts' feed-forward weights, around 13B active parameters. Compute per token tracks active parameters, so speed is close to a 13B model. But all 47B must sit in memory, so hardware requirements look like a big model.
keyPoints: All experts must be in memory
Fast like small, memory like large

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Your flagship is a sparse MoE with about ten times more total than active parameters. Why does that suit private enterprise deployment, and where does it hurt?
items.answer: Enterprises get large-model quality at small-model compute per token, which keeps latency and per-request cost down on their own GPUs. It hurts on memory: every expert has to be loaded, so you need more GPU memory than the active size suggests, and small batch sizes leave experts underused. Expert parallelism across GPUs adds networking demands.
keyPoints: High quality at low per-token compute
Low batch sizes waste expert capacity

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: A family ships a 30B MoE with about 3B active and a 32B dense model. When would you pick the MoE?
items.answer: Pick the MoE when throughput and latency per token matter most and you have memory for all 30B weights: it runs at roughly 3B-model speed. Pick the dense model when you want the best quality per parameter, are memory-limited relative to compute, or plan to fine-tune (dense models are simpler to tune and serve). Benchmark both on your task before deciding.
keyPoints: MoE: fast per token, needs full memory
Fine-tuning and serving are simpler on dense

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: A model has 355B total but 32B active parameters. What does that split buy and what does it cost?
items.answer: It buys capacity to store more knowledge and skills while each token costs about as much as a 32B dense model, so serving throughput is good. It costs memory (all 355B weights across GPUs), complex expert-parallel serving, and routing imbalance. Training also needs care to keep experts balanced and specialised.
keyPoints: Knowledge capacity of a large model

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How does a fine-grained MoE with shared experts differ from a standard top-2 MoE?
items.answer: Instead of a few large experts, it uses many smaller experts and activates more of them per token, which allows more flexible combinations of specialisations at the same compute. It also adds one or more shared experts that every token passes through, capturing common knowledge so the routed experts can specialise. The result is better quality for the same active parameters.
keyPoints: Many small experts, more activated per token

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What was wrong with auxiliary load-balancing losses in MoE, and how does a bias-based, loss-free approach fix it?
items.answer: An auxiliary loss pushes the router toward even expert usage, but it competes with the language modelling loss and can hurt quality. The loss-free approach adds a per-expert bias to routing scores only for selecting experts, nudging the bias down for overloaded experts and up for underused ones after each step. Balance improves without a gradient that fights the main objective.
keyPoints: Aux loss trades quality for balance
Bias added only for expert selection

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Implement a top-k MoE router in PyTorch and point out the efficiency and correctness traps.
items.answer: Compute router logits with a linear layer, take top-k per token, softmax over the chosen scores, then group tokens by expert, run each expert on its batch and scatter-add weighted outputs back. Traps: looping per token instead of batching per expert, capacity overflow and dropped tokens, numerically unstable softmax in low precision, and forgetting that a shared expert adds its output for every token.
keyPoints: Linear router, top-k, softmax over chosen
Gather tokens per expert, scatter back

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Why did transformers replace RNNs for language modelling, and what does the KV cache buy you at inference?
items.answer: RNNs process tokens one after another, which blocks parallel training and makes long-range dependencies hard. Attention looks at all positions directly and trains in parallel on GPUs, so transformers scale far better. At inference, the KV cache stores past keys and values so each new token only computes its own, turning repeated work into a lookup.
keyPoints: RNNs are sequential and forget long range
KV cache avoids recomputing past tokens

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Explain self-attention. What is its computational cost, and what are your options when contexts get long?
items.answer: Each token attends to every other, so compute and memory grow quadratically with sequence length. Options: memory-efficient exact kernels such as FlashAttention, sliding-window or sparse attention, grouped or latent KV compression to shrink the cache, and position schemes that extrapolate. At the application level, retrieve or summarise instead of feeding everything.
keyPoints: O(n^2) compute and memory in length
Retrieval or summarisation at app level

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Explain the architecture choices in a Llama-class model: why grouped-query attention, RoPE and SwiGLU instead of the original 2017 transformer?
items.answer: GQA shrinks the KV cache so long contexts and large batches are cheaper to serve. RoPE encodes relative position by rotating queries and keys, which generalises better and supports context extension. SwiGLU, a gated feed-forward activation, gives better quality per parameter than ReLU. Pre-normalisation with RMSNorm also makes deep stacks train more stably.
keyPoints: GQA for a smaller KV cache
RoPE for relative positions and extension

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What is SwiGLU and why did gated activations replace ReLU and GELU in LLM feed-forward blocks?
items.answer: SwiGLU splits the feed-forward projection in two: one branch passes through a Swish activation and gates the other by elementwise multiplication. The gate lets the network control information flow per dimension, which empirically improves quality at the same compute. To keep parameters equal, the hidden size is usually reduced to about two-thirds.
keyPoints: Two projections, one gates the other
Hidden size shrunk to match parameters

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Why do modern transformers put normalisation before each block, and what is RMSNorm?
items.answer: Pre-norm normalises inputs to attention and feed-forward sub-layers while keeping a clean residual path, so gradients flow through deep stacks and training is more stable with less warm-up tuning. RMSNorm rescales by the root mean square without subtracting the mean or using a bias, which is cheaper and works as well in practice.
keyPoints: Pre-norm keeps the residual path clean
RMSNorm scales by root mean square only

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Walk through one forward pass of a decoder-only transformer, tensor by tensor.
items.answer: Token ids of shape (batch, seq) index the embedding table to give (batch, seq, d_model). Each block normalises, projects to Q, K, V of shape (batch, heads, seq, d_head), applies positions (for example RoPE), runs masked attention, projects back and adds the residual; then normalises again and runs the feed-forward network with another residual. A final norm and the unembedding matrix give logits of shape (batch, seq, vocab).
keyPoints: Q, K, V per head with positions
FFN, final norm, logits (B, T, V)

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What are the key components of a transformer model and why does each matter?
items.answer: Embeddings turn tokens into vectors; positional encoding injects order; self-attention lets tokens use context; feed-forward layers store and transform knowledge per token; residual connections and normalisation keep deep stacks trainable; and the output head maps to vocabulary probabilities. Most parameters live in the feed-forward and attention projections, which is why parameter counts track model capacity.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Explain attention-free sequence architectures and their trade-offs.
items.answer: State-space models and linear-attention or recurrent variants replace quadratic attention with a fixed-size state updated per token, so compute grows linearly and decoding memory is constant. They handle very long sequences cheaply but tend to be weaker at exact recall and copying from far back in context. Hybrid models mix a few attention layers with these layers to get most of both.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: A 7B model combined grouped-query attention with sliding-window attention. What does each buy and cost?
items.answer: GQA reduces KV heads, so the cache and memory bandwidth shrink and decoding gets faster, with a small quality cost. Sliding-window attention limits each layer to the last W tokens, making attention cost linear in length and allowing a fixed-size rolling cache; stacking layers still lets information travel further than W. The cost is weaker direct access to distant tokens.
keyPoints: Sliding window: linear cost, rolling cache
Distant tokens are seen only indirectly

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What is the difference between pretraining, supervised fine-tuning and preference optimisation?
items.answer: Pretraining learns language and knowledge by next-token prediction over huge unlabelled text. Supervised fine-tuning trains on curated prompt and response pairs so the model follows instructions in the desired format. Preference optimisation (RLHF, DPO and similar) uses comparisons between responses to push the model toward outputs people prefer, such as more helpful or safer answers.
keyPoints: Pretraining: broad knowledge from raw text
Each stage uses less but costlier data

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How are cross-entropy, KL divergence and perplexity related, and why is cross-entropy the training loss for language models?
items.answer: Cross-entropy between the data distribution and the model equals the data's entropy plus the KL divergence from data to model, so minimising cross-entropy minimises KL since the entropy term is fixed. Perplexity is the exponential of average per-token cross-entropy, an interpretable 'effective branching factor'. Cross-entropy is also the negative log-likelihood, so minimising it is maximum likelihood training.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Your pretraining loss suddenly diverges at step 300k of a long run. Diagnose and fix it.
items.answer: Check whether a bad data shard arrived (look at the batches just before), then at gradient norms, attention logit growth and loss-scale or overflow events in low precision. Roll back to a checkpoint before the spike, skip or fix the offending data, and stabilise with lower learning rate, tighter gradient clipping, QK normalisation or z-loss on logits. Monitor per-layer statistics so you catch the next one earlier.
keyPoints: Inspect data just before the spike
Gradient norms, logit growth, precision overflows
Roll back, skip data, lower LR or clip

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Loss spikes mid-run on a large pretraining job. Walk through how you debug it.
items.answer: Correlate the spike with data (shard, domain, sequence length), optimizer state (Adam second-moment collapse, learning-rate schedule changes) and hardware (a node producing bad gradients). Reproduce from the previous checkpoint with the same data order. Common fixes are skipping bad batches, rewinding, reducing LR, clipping, and logit stabilisation; record the incident so automated rollback can handle future ones.
keyPoints: Correlate with data, optimizer and hardware

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What breaks when you scale LLM training from 8 GPUs to thousands, and how do modern stacks cope?
items.answer: The model and optimizer state no longer fit on one device, communication starts to dominate, and hardware failures become routine. Stacks combine data parallelism with sharded optimizer state (ZeRO or FSDP), tensor and pipeline parallelism, and overlap communication with compute. They checkpoint frequently, detect and replace failing nodes automatically, and keep data loading deterministic so runs can resume exactly.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: You are building a web-scale pretraining corpus. Walk through the pipeline and how you decide whether each filter earns its place.
items.answer: Extract text from crawled pages, identify language, apply heuristic quality filters (length, symbol ratios, repetition), remove personal data, deduplicate at document and near-duplicate level, and optionally score with a quality classifier. Decide on each filter by ablation: train small models on data with and without it and compare downstream benchmark scores, keeping filters that improve results per token.
keyPoints: Keep filters that win small-model ablations

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design a deduplication pipeline for a web-scale pretraining corpus that runs as a streaming process.
items.answer: Exact duplicates are cheap with content hashes. For near duplicates, compute MinHash signatures over shingles and use locality-sensitive hashing bands to find candidate matches, keeping a sharded index of seen signatures so new documents are checked as they stream in. Decide which copy to keep, track false positive rates on samples, and dedup across crawls too.
keyPoints: MinHash plus LSH for near duplicates

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How do you build a training dataset without causing model collapse when much of the data is synthetic?
items.answer: Collapse happens when models train repeatedly on their own outputs and the distribution narrows, losing rare cases. Keep a strong share of real human data, filter synthetic data hard with verifiers or reward models, generate from diverse prompts and models, and track diversity metrics. Prefer synthetic data that can be checked, such as code with tests or maths with answers.
keyPoints: Keep real data in the mix

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Walk through a post-training recipe that turns a pretrained base model into a personalised assistant.
items.answer: Start with SFT on high-quality instruction and chat data in the target style, then preference tuning (DPO or RLHF) on comparisons for helpfulness and safety, plus targeted data for tool use and refusal behaviour. For personalisation, add memory or user context at inference rather than per-user weights, and evaluate on helpfulness, safety and personalisation quality with regression checks after each stage.
keyPoints: Preference tuning for helpfulness and safety
Personalise through context, evaluate each stage

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What is multi-token prediction and why train with it?
items.answer: Besides predicting the next token, extra heads or modules predict tokens further ahead. This densifies the training signal and encourages representations that plan ahead, which can improve quality. At inference the extra heads can be used as a draft for speculative decoding, speeding up generation, or dropped entirely.
keyPoints: Extra heads can drive speculative decoding

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: One model family pretrained with autoregressive blank infilling. How does that differ from BERT and GPT objectives?
items.answer: BERT masks individual tokens and predicts them bidirectionally, which is good for understanding but not generation. GPT predicts left to right, which is good for generation. Blank infilling masks spans and regenerates them autoregressively while the unmasked context is visible bidirectionally, aiming to support both understanding and generation in one objective.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What is the KV cache, what are its memory implications at scale, and what is the formula for its size?
items.answer: During decoding, each layer stores the keys and values of all previous tokens so new tokens do not recompute them. Size is 2 (K and V) x layers x KV heads x head dimension x sequence length x batch x bytes per value. It grows linearly with context and batch and often exceeds the weights at long context, which limits concurrency; GQA, MLA, quantised caches and paging reduce it.
keyPoints: Stores past K and V per layer
2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x seq x batch x bytes
GQA, MLA, quantisation and paging shrink it

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Explain the prefill and decode phases. Why is prefill compute-bound and decode memory-bandwidth-bound?
items.answer: Prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel as big matrix multiplies, so the GPU's arithmetic units are the limit and it sets time to first token. Decode generates one token at a time per sequence, so every step reads all weights and the KV cache from memory for very little compute, making memory bandwidth the limit. Batching many sequences during decode raises arithmetic intensity.
keyPoints: Prefill: parallel matmuls, compute-bound, sets TTFT
Decode: one token per step, bandwidth-bound
Each decode step re-reads weights and cache

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What are TTFT, TPOT, inter-token latency and throughput, and how do they trade against each other?
items.answer: TTFT is time to first token (queueing plus prefill). TPOT or inter-token latency is the time per generated token during decode. Throughput is total tokens per second across all users. Larger batches raise throughput but slow each user's tokens and can delay TTFT; long prompts raise TTFT. Set targets per use case, for example a chat UI cares most about TTFT and steady streaming.
keyPoints: TPOT and ITL: decode speed per user
Batching trades per-user speed for throughput

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Do the roofline maths: roughly how many tokens per second can one H100 produce for a 70B model at batch size 1?
items.answer: At batch 1 decoding is memory-bound: each token reads all weights. In FP16 a 70B model is about 140 GB, which does not even fit in one 80 GB H100, so you need 8-bit or lower; at 8-bit that is about 70 GB. With roughly 3.35 TB/s of bandwidth, the ceiling is about 3350 / 70, around 45 to 50 tokens per second before overheads. Bigger batches reuse each weight read across sequences, which is why throughput rises with batch.
keyPoints: 70B FP16 = 140 GB, does not fit one H100
Ceiling around 45 to 50 tok/s; batching amortises reads

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Estimate the KV-cache memory to serve a 70B-class model at 128k context. What do you do when it does not fit?
items.answer: Take a Llama-70B-like shape: 80 layers, 8 KV heads with GQA, head dimension 128, FP16. Per token that is 2 x 80 x 8 x 128 x 2 bytes, about 0.33 MB, so 128k tokens is roughly 40 GB for a single sequence. Options: quantise the cache to 8 or 4 bits, use paged allocation, offload cold blocks to CPU, shard across GPUs, cap context per tier, or use retrieval instead of full context.
keyPoints: Per token: 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes
About 0.33 MB per token, about 40 GB at 128k

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Our serving cost is dominated by the KV cache, not the weights. Cut it by an order of magnitude and say what you give up.
items.answer: Stack several reductions: multi-query or grouped attention to cut KV heads, sliding-window attention in most layers with only a few global layers, sharing KV across adjacent layers, and quantising the cache to int8. Add prefix caching so repeated history is reused. You give up some long-range recall and quality, which you must measure on long conversations.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Estimate what one chat message costs to serve, and say which lever moves it most.
items.answer: Cost per message is roughly GPU cost per second times GPU-seconds per message. GPU-seconds depend on prompt tokens (prefill, reduced by prefix caching) and output tokens (decode, shared across the batch). With long chat histories, prefill of the history dominates unless cached, so prefix caching and KV-cache size are usually the biggest levers, followed by batch size and quantisation.
keyPoints: GPU cost x GPU-seconds per message
Prefill of history plus decode of reply
Prefix caching often the biggest lever

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Explain FlashAttention. It does not reduce FLOPs, so why is it faster?
items.answer: Standard attention writes the full sequence-by-sequence score matrix to GPU high-bandwidth memory and reads it back, so it is limited by memory traffic. FlashAttention tiles the computation so blocks of Q, K and V stay in fast on-chip SRAM, computing softmax incrementally with running maxima and sums, and never materialises the full matrix. Same maths, far less memory traffic, and memory use becomes linear in sequence length.
keyPoints: Exact result with less memory movement

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How would you reduce inference time for an LLM application?
items.answer: Measure first: split time into queueing, prefill and decode. Then reduce work (shorter prompts, prompt caching, fewer output tokens, smaller or distilled models, routing easy requests to them) and make the work faster (quantisation, efficient serving engines with continuous batching and paged KV cache, speculative decoding). Stream tokens to cut perceived latency and parallelise independent calls.
keyPoints: Less work: shorter prompts, smaller models
Faster work: quantise, better engine, speculative decoding

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: Estimate the KV cache for serving a 7B model with sliding-window attention, and design the rolling-buffer cache that the window allows.
items.answer: Per token: 2 x 32 layers x 8 KV heads x 128 dims x 2 bytes, about 128 KB. With a 4096-token window, each sequence only ever needs the last 4096 positions, so the cache is a fixed ring buffer of that size per layer (about 0.5 GB per sequence) regardless of total length. Writes go to position i mod W, and attention masks account for wrap-around order.
keyPoints: About 128 KB per token for this shape
Window caps cache at W tokens
Ring buffer indexed by position mod W

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Compare greedy decoding, beam search, top-k, top-p and temperature sampling. When does each fail?
items.answer: Greedy picks the highest-probability token each step: deterministic but prone to repetition. Beam search keeps several candidate sequences: good for short, constrained outputs like translation but bland for open text. Temperature rescales the distribution (lower is sharper), top-k samples from the k best tokens, and top-p from the smallest set covering probability p. Too much randomness causes incoherence, too little causes loops.
keyPoints: Beam: good for constrained tasks, bland otherwise
Top-k and top-p truncate the tail

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Implement temperature, top-k and top-p sampling over a vector of logits.
items.answer: Divide logits by temperature (treat 0 as argmax). For top-k, keep the k largest logits and set the rest to negative infinity. For top-p, sort probabilities descending, take the cumulative sum and keep the smallest prefix whose sum reaches p (always at least one token). Softmax the survivors stably and sample with a seeded RNG for tests.
keyPoints: Top-p keeps the smallest prefix reaching p

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How do you adjust how creative a generative model's output is?
items.answer: Raise temperature or top-p for more varied output, lower them for focused, repeatable answers. Prompting matters as much: ask for several distinct options, give style examples, or set constraints. Pick settings per task (low for extraction and code, higher for brainstorming) and evaluate, since some reasoning models fix or ignore these parameters.
keyPoints: Prompts can ask for diverse options
Low for factual tasks, higher for ideation

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: Explain temperature in LLMs.
items.answer: Temperature scales logits before the softmax. Values below 1 sharpen the distribution so the most likely tokens dominate; above 1 flatten it so unlikely tokens appear more often; near 0 is effectively greedy. It changes randomness, not knowledge, so it will not fix hallucinations, and repeated calls at temperature 0 can still differ slightly on some providers.
keyPoints: Near zero is close to greedy

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: What are top-k, top-p, temperature and the other common LLM generation parameters?
items.answer: Temperature controls randomness; top-k limits sampling to the k most likely tokens; top-p limits it to the smallest set covering probability p. Max tokens caps output length, stop sequences end generation, and frequency or presence penalties discourage repetition. Seeds, when supported, make sampling more reproducible.

source.title: ZS LLM Engineer interview experience (GeeksforGeeks)

items.question: Implement beam search for an autoregressive model. When would an answer engine actually use it?
items.answer: Keep the B best partial sequences by total log-probability. At each step expand each with its top candidates, score them, keep the best B, and move finished sequences (end token) aside; apply length normalisation so short outputs are not unfairly favoured.
