items.answer: The server stores the computed attention state (KV cache) for a prompt prefix so later requests starting with the same tokens skip recomputing it, cutting latency and cost. It pays off with long, stable prefixes such as system prompts, tool definitions and documents. Any change in the prefix tokens, including timestamps, reordered tools or user-specific text near the start, invalidates the cache.
keyPoints: Reuse KV state for identical prefixes

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: A chat assistant re-sends the whole conversation each turn. How do you avoid recomputing it, and what are the pitfalls?
items.answer: Use prefix caching so the unchanged history is reused, and append new turns at the end. Pitfalls: anything that edits earlier text (re-summarising, inserting timestamps) invalidates the cache, cache lifetimes are limited, and cache entries consume memory. Design context assembly so the stable part is byte-identical between turns.
keyPoints: Edits or timestamps break the cache

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: You have eight hours to build a coding agent from scratch. What do you build, and more importantly, what do you cut?
items.answer: Build the smallest loop that works end to end: a model call with a handful of tools (read, search, edit, run command), a step budget, and test feedback. Cut multi-agent orchestration, fancy memory, UI polish and broad language support. Spend the saved time on evaluation tasks so you can see whether changes help.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: You are training an agent model with end-to-end reinforcement learning in your own harness. Walk through the environment and reward design.
items.answer: Create environments that mirror real tasks (repos with tests), with a harness identical to production so training matches deployment. Reward verifiable outcomes such as tests passing, add small shaping for efficiency, and guard against reward hacking (editing tests, hard-coding outputs) with hidden tests and diff checks. Monitor rollouts for exploits and keep a held-out evaluation set.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How do AI evals work?
items.answer: You define the behaviour you care about, build a dataset of representative inputs (with expected answers or rubrics), run the system, and score outputs with code checks, human review or an LLM judge. Results are tracked across versions to catch regressions, and failures from production feed back into the dataset. Evals replace guessing with measurement.

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: How do you evaluate a generative AI system?
items.answer: Split evaluation by layer: component metrics (retrieval recall, tool accuracy), end-to-end quality (correctness, faithfulness, helpfulness), safety, and operational metrics (latency, cost). Use a golden dataset plus LLM judges calibrated against human labels, run it in CI, and complement it with online monitoring and user feedback.

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: What methods and metrics do you use to evaluate how well an LLM performs?
items.answer: Match the metric to the task: exact match or F1 for extraction, pass rate for code, groundedness and answer relevance for RAG, rubric or pairwise comparisons for open-ended writing, plus safety and robustness checks. Benchmarks give a rough ranking, but decisions should rest on a task-specific set with agreed thresholds, along with latency and cost.
keyPoints: Pass rate for code, groundedness for RAG

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: Design an LLM-as-judge evaluation. What are its known biases and how do you correct for them?
items.answer: Write a clear rubric, ask for reasoning then a score, and use pairwise comparison or reference answers where possible. Known biases: preferring longer answers, favouring its own model family, position bias (preferring the first answer), and over-trusting fluent text. Randomise order, normalise for length, use a different judge model, and calibrate against human labels on a sample.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How do you build an evaluation set when there is no labelled ground truth and experts are expensive?
items.answer: Start from real queries or logs, have the model draft candidate answers or questions from documents, then have experts review a smaller sample and fix labels. Use synthetic generation for coverage, active selection to spend expert time on ambiguous or high-risk cases, and measure judge agreement with the expert sample before relying on automatic scoring.
keyPoints: Spend expert time on risky cases

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Your annotators have no ground truth because the task is subjective preference. How do you measure and improve label quality?
items.answer: Measure inter-annotator agreement (for example Cohen's or Krippendorff's kappa) and gold-question accuracy, look at per-annotator consistency and bias, and use guidelines with examples. Improve with calibration sessions, adjudication of disagreements, redundancy on hard items, and filtering or retraining low-quality annotators. Accept that some disagreement is signal, not noise.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design online evaluation: what do you log, what do you sample, and what do you A/B test?
items.answer: Log inputs, retrieved context, outputs, tool calls, latency, cost and user feedback with privacy controls. Sample traffic for automated judging and human review, oversampling low-confidence or negative-feedback cases. A/B test changes to prompts, models and retrieval with guardrail metrics for safety and latency, and feed discovered failures back into the offline set.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: An evaluation pipeline you own suddenly reports a six-point drop for a customer's model between Tuesday and Wednesday, although the model did not change. Debug it.
items.answer: Check what else changed: the judge model or version, prompts, dataset version, scoring code, API behaviour or sampling parameters. Re-run Tuesday's inputs on Tuesday's config to see if the drop reproduces, diff outputs for a few items, and look at variance across seeds. Fix by pinning judge and harness versions and logging all of them with each run.
keyPoints: List everything that could have changed
Pin and log judge and harness versions

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Why do benchmark scores improve while users say the system got worse? Enumerate the reasons.
items.answer: Benchmarks may not match real tasks or distributions, models may overfit or be contaminated, scores average away regressions in important slices, tone, latency or cost may have worsened, evaluation harness settings may differ from production, and users care about things benchmarks do not capture. Add task-specific evals and slice analysis and watch online signals.
keyPoints: Latency, cost, tone and harness differences

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How would you evaluate an autonomous software engineering agent? Explain why benchmark pass rates can mislead.
items.answer: Use a suite of realistic tasks with hidden tests, measure resolved rate, cost, time and the quality of changes (review acceptance, regressions introduced). Public pass rates can mislead because tasks may be contaminated, tests can be weak so wrong patches pass, setups differ from real repositories, and scores ignore effort and review burden.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How would you build the evaluation suite to confirm an AI agent meets its accuracy and cost targets?
items.answer: Define target metrics (task success, tool accuracy, cost per task, latency), then build a dataset of representative and edge-case tasks with graders, including failure injection. Run each task several times to measure variance, report success against cost, and gate releases on thresholds in CI. Add production failures to the set over time.
keyPoints: Targets for success, cost and latency
CI gate; grow from production failures

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: Design the regression gate that decides whether a prompt or model change ships.
items.answer: Run a versioned eval suite on the candidate and the baseline with the same settings, compare overall and per-slice metrics with confidence intervals, and check safety, latency and cost. Block on any critical regression, require review of borderline cases, record results with the change, and roll out gradually with monitoring.
keyPoints: Same suite for candidate and baseline

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Build the evaluation harness for a new frontier model release. What does it need to do?
items.answer: Run a broad battery (capabilities, safety, robustness, long context, multilingual) at scale and reproducibly, with fixed prompts and settings, contamination controls, and statistical reporting. It should compare against prior models, support human evaluation for subjective areas, track versions, and produce a report the release decision can rest on.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: A customer wants to deploy your RAG system but has no labelled data. How do you evaluate it before and after launch?
items.answer: Before launch, collect real questions from users, generate and expert-review a starter set, and measure retrieval recall and answer groundedness with judges calibrated on a small human-labelled sample. After launch, monitor feedback, sample and review answers, track unsupported-claim rates and no-answer cases, and keep adding failures to the dataset.
keyPoints: Real questions plus reviewed synthetic set
Sampled review and feedback after launch

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How do you detect and measure hallucinations in a production RAG system?
items.answer: Check faithfulness by decomposing answers into claims and verifying each against the retrieved context with an entailment model or judge. Sample production traffic, measure the unsupported-claim rate, track user reports, and separate retrieval failures (missing evidence) from generation failures (ignoring evidence). Alert on rate changes and add cases to the eval set.
keyPoints: Sample traffic and track the rate

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How would you evaluate an agent, as opposed to a single model response?
items.answer: Evaluate the whole trajectory as well as the final answer: did it choose the right tools, with correct arguments, in a sensible order, recover from errors, and stay within permissions and budgets. Use tasks with checkable end states, repeat runs for variance, and include injected failures. Report success rate alongside cost and steps.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How would you benchmark an LLM agent's tool use for enterprise workflows that compose ten or more APIs?
items.answer: Build simulated or sandboxed versions of the APIs with deterministic state, write tasks with a checkable final state, and measure success, correct tool sequences, argument accuracy and robustness to errors and distractor tools. Include ambiguous requests and permission boundaries, and run enough repeats to separate model skill from luck.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: You are taking a working GenAI agent prototype to production for an enterprise. What is your checklist between demo and launch?
items.answer: Evaluation on realistic tasks with success thresholds, guardrails and permission limits, security review including prompt-injection tests, observability and tracing, cost and latency budgets, fallbacks and human escalation, load testing, rollout plan with canary and rollback, and an owner for monitoring and incident response.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How would you approach designing a system to ensure the safe deployment of AI models in production?
items.answer: Threat-model first, then layer controls: least-privilege tools, input and output filtering, human approval for risky actions, rate limits and monitoring, and red-team testing before launch. Evaluate safety as part of the release gate, keep audit logs, define an incident response plan, and monitor for misuse and drift after launch.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What is prompt injection (direct and indirect), and what is your layered defence?
items.answer: Direct injection is a user trying to override instructions; indirect injection hides instructions in content the model reads, such as web pages, emails or documents. Defend in layers: treat all retrieved content as data, limit what tools can do, require approval for sensitive actions, filter inputs and outputs, isolate untrusted content, block data exfiltration channels (such as rendering external image URLs), and test continuously.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: An assistant summarises incoming email. An attacker emails a target with hidden instructions addressed to the model. Walk through the attack and your defence.
items.answer: The hidden text could tell the assistant to forward data, change settings or insert malicious links in summaries. Defence: mark email content as untrusted, never let it trigger tool calls on its own, restrict the assistant to read-only unless the user confirms, strip or neutralise hidden text, block automatic external requests, scan outputs for exfiltration patterns, and red-team with such emails.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How do you stop an agent with tool access from leaking data through a malicious web page?
items.answer: Break the lethal combination of private data, untrusted content and an outbound channel. Restrict network egress to allow-listed domains, strip or confirm links and image loads that could carry data in URLs, sandbox browsing from sensitive context, require confirmation before sending data externally, and monitor outgoing requests.
keyPoints: Private data plus untrusted content plus exit path

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design guardrails for a consumer-facing assistant. Input filters, output filters, or both?
items.answer: Both, plus policy in the system prompt and limits in tools. Input filters catch abuse and obvious attacks early and cheaply; output filters catch what slipped through and enforce format and policy before the user sees it. Measure false positives as carefully as false negatives, log blocks, and tune with red-team data.
keyPoints: Log and tune with red-team data

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What is the difference between jailbreaking and prompt injection?
items.answer: Jailbreaking is a user trying to get the model to violate its safety policy, for example by role-play tricks. Prompt injection is smuggling instructions into the model's input, often through third-party content, to make an application behave in unintended ways. Jailbreaks target the model's rules; injections target the application's trust boundaries.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design the safety system for open-ended character chat.
items.answer: Combine classifiers on user input and model output (self-harm, sexual content, violence, grooming), policy-aware system prompts, age-aware experiences, crisis resources and escalation, rate limits and reporting tools. Consider intervening during generation for severe categories, and evaluate with red-teaming, human review and monitoring of incident rates.
keyPoints: Intervention during generation for severe cases

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How would you design safeguards for an AI system that takes actions on behalf of a user?
items.answer: Give it least-privilege, scoped credentials; classify actions by risk and require explicit confirmation for irreversible or costly ones; validate arguments outside the model; rate-limit and budget actions; log everything for audit; and provide undo where possible. Evaluate with adversarial tests, including injection through content the agent reads.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: As agents become powerful enough to act on a user's behalf, how do you decide which actions to automate and which to keep under human oversight?
items.answer: Score actions on reversibility, blast radius, cost, regulatory impact and the agent's measured reliability. Automate low-risk, reversible, well-tested actions; require approval for high-impact ones; and start conservative, expanding autonomy as evidence accumulates. Make the boundary configurable and revisit it with incident data.

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: Design permission-aware retrieval: users must never see content they cannot access in the source system.
items.answer: Ingest each document's access control list with the content and enforce it at query time as a filter inside the retrieval engine, not after generation. Keep permissions fresh through change events, handle group membership resolution, and test with cross-tenant and revoked-access cases. Never cache answers across users without keying by permission scope.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Two partners at the same firm are on opposite sides of a deal. Design the data isolation on top of normal multi-tenancy.
items.answer: Add ethical walls as first-class access rules: matters have explicit membership, retrieval and caches are scoped to matter-level permissions, and the model never sees data outside the user's allowed set. Isolate indexes or enforce mandatory filters, log access, and test by attempting cross-wall queries. Cached or learned artifacts must not carry data across walls.
keyPoints: Mandatory scoped filters or separate indexes

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How would you prevent personal data from reaching an external model?
items.answer: Detect and redact or tokenise PII before the request leaves your boundary, using pattern and ML detectors, and reverse the substitution on the response if needed. Minimise what you send, use providers with zero-retention terms and private connectivity, keep PII out of logs, and test detectors for misses.
keyPoints: Detect and redact or tokenise before sending
No PII in logs; test detectors

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: PHI is in every audio file, transcript and note you touch. How does that shape the architecture, and what can you send to a third-party model API?
items.answer: Treat PHI as the design constraint: encryption in transit and at rest, strict access control and audit, minimal retention, and regional residency. Only send PHI to vendors under a business associate agreement with no training use and zero retention, otherwise de-identify first. Keep PHI out of logs and analytics.
keyPoints: Vendors only under BAAs, no training

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How do you keep users' data safe and private when building AI systems?
items.answer: Collect and retain as little as possible, encrypt and restrict access, redact sensitive data before it reaches models or logs, give users control and deletion, and choose model providers with appropriate data-handling terms. Test for leakage (memorisation, cross-user bleed) and document practices for audits.

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: Design a red-teaming programme for a model or application you are about to release.
items.answer: Define harm categories and threat actors, build a library of attack prompts (direct, indirect, multi-turn, obfuscated), mix automated attack generation with human experts, and test the whole system including tools and retrieval. Record attack success rates, triage by severity, fix, and convert findings into regression tests that run on every release.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: A feature that summarises job applicants is accused of working worse for some groups. How do you establish whether that is true, and what do you do?
items.answer: Define the harm and fairness metric, assemble evaluation data with group labels where legally and ethically possible, and compare quality and outcomes across groups with confidence intervals. If a gap exists, find causes (data, prompts, model), fix and re-test, add monitoring, keep humans responsible for decisions, and document findings and limits.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How do you think about AI safety, ethics, guardrails and governance in practice?
items.answer: Treat them as engineering practices: risk assessments before launch, evaluations for harmful behaviour and bias, technical guardrails, human oversight for high-stakes use, transparency about limits, incident response, and governance mapping to regulations. Tie each principle to a concrete control and a metric.

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: What are the ethical risks of deploying agentic AI systems in high-stakes environments?
items.answer: Unintended or irreversible actions, accountability gaps, bias in decisions, over-reliance and deskilling, privacy and security exposure, and difficulty auditing long trajectories. Mitigate with human oversight, narrow permissions, thorough testing, transparency, monitoring and clear ownership for outcomes.

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: Design Slack, with follow-ups at 100x and 1000x scale and for global users.
items.answer: Clarify features (channels, DMs, search, presence), then design: clients over websockets, a gateway, message service writing to a partitioned store, fan-out to channel members, and a search index. At higher scale, shard by workspace or channel, use queues for fan-out, regional deployments and caches for hot channels, and consider eventual consistency for presence. State bottlenecks and trade-offs as numbers grow.

source.title: OpenAI software engineer interview guide (Aced, formerly Exponent)

items.question: Design a developer playground for a hosted LLM API, from the UI down to the architecture.
items.answer: A web UI for prompts, parameters and model choice sends requests through an authenticated backend that calls the model service, streams tokens back over server-sent events, and stores conversations and presets. Add rate limits and quotas, usage metering, safety filters, and sharing features. Discuss streaming reliability, cost control and logging without leaking user data.

source.title: OpenAI software engineer interview guide (Aced, formerly Exponent)

items.question: Design the serving stack for a consumer chat assistant at hundreds of millions of users.
items.answer: Edge and API gateway with auth and rate limits; a router that picks model tiers; inference clusters with continuous batching, paged KV cache and prefix caching; streaming responses; autoscaling on queue depth and GPU utilisation; regional deployment and failover; usage metering; safety filters; and observability. Discuss p99 latency versus utilisation, capacity planning and graceful degradation under load.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Define the strategy and a single key metric for an internal AI platform that other teams build agents on.
items.answer: Strategy: provide shared, secure building blocks (model access, tool and data connectors, evaluation, observability, guardrails) so teams ship faster and safer. A good single metric is the number of agents or use cases running in production that meet a quality bar, or time from idea to production, paired with guardrail metrics for cost and incidents.
keyPoints: Single metric tied to adoption in production

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: Design an assistant that answers questions over a user's email, documents and meetings without ever leaking content the user cannot access.
items.answer: Index each source with per-item access control lists, enforce permissions at retrieval using the user's identity, resolve group membership at query time, and never use caches shared across users. Rank with recency and relevance, cite sources, and test with revoked-access and shared-folder edge cases. Log access for audit.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design a text-to-SQL system over a warehouse with thousands of tables.
items.answer: Retrieve only relevant tables and columns using schema descriptions, sample values and usage statistics, supply a curated semantic layer or metric definitions, and generate SQL with the model. Validate by parsing, checking permissions, running with limits on a read-only role, and optionally verifying results. Evaluate on a question set with known answers and learn from user corrections.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How does an answer engine handle breaking news, a query about something that happened 20 minutes ago?
items.answer: Use live search with freshness-weighted ranking and fast crawlers or news feeds for recent content, bypass stale caches for time-sensitive queries, prefer reputable sources, and show timestamps. The model should say when information is developing or conflicting, and quote sources rather than rely on its training data.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design the retrieval pipeline for 100 billion web pages with sub-second latency and freshness guarantees.
items.answer: Sharded inverted and vector indexes distributed across many machines, tiered by freshness and popularity, with a fast tier for recent content. Queries fan out in parallel with deadlines, candidates are merged and reranked in stages, and crawling prioritises pages by change rate. Use caching and approximate indexes, and accept partial results at the latency deadline.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design an LLM gateway with routing across providers, failover, caching, budgets and rate limits.
items.answer: A single API in front of all providers that authenticates callers, applies per-team budgets and rate limits, routes by model, cost or availability, retries and fails over with circuit breakers, caches eligible requests, and logs usage and latency. Normalise request and response formats, handle streaming, and keep the gateway itself highly available since it is on the critical path.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design the routing layer that decides whether a request is handled on-device, by a first-party server model, or by a third-party model.
items.answer: Route on task complexity, privacy sensitivity, latency, connectivity and user consent: simple private tasks stay on-device, heavier ones go to a secure server model, and only requests that need world knowledge or capability go to a third party with explicit consent and minimal data. A classifier or rules decide, with fallbacks if a tier fails and telemetry that respects privacy.
keyPoints: Third party only with consent and minimisation

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How would you cut LLM serving cost by 10x? List the levers and rank them.
items.answer: Biggest first: route easy requests to smaller models, shorten prompts and outputs, cache (exact, semantic, prefix), then serving efficiency such as continuous batching, quantisation, speculative decoding and better GPU utilisation, and finally negotiated pricing or cheaper hardware. Measure each against quality, because savings that hurt quality are not savings.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: A chat feature has a p95 budget of 3 seconds to first useful content. Where does the time go, and how do you cut it?
items.answer: Break it into network and gateway, auth, retrieval, reranking, prompt building, queueing, model prefill, and first decode token. Measure each at p95, then cut: parallelise retrieval calls, cache static context, shrink prompts, use a faster or smaller model for the first token, stream immediately, and pre-warm connections.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Your p99 latency doubled after a deploy with no model change. Walk through the diagnosis.
items.answer: Compare traces before and after to see which stage grew, then check what changed in the deploy: prompt length, retrieval settings, new middleware, dependency versions, cache hit rate, batching configuration or autoscaling. Check queue depth and GPU utilisation, tail amplification from retries, and noisy neighbours. Roll back if impact is severe, then fix and add a latency regression test.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: p95 time to first token regressed from 1.2 s to 3 s after a release. Find and fix it.
items.answer: Break time to first token into queueing, retrieval and prefill. Compare prompt token counts and cache hit rates before and after, check retrieval latency and batching or scheduler settings, and look at GPU saturation. Typical culprits are longer prompts, a lost prefix cache, extra serial calls, or a scheduler change. Fix the cause and alert on the metric.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design the scheduler for a continuous-batching inference engine.
items.answer: Maintain waiting and running queues. Each iteration, admit new requests while memory and token budgets allow, run one decode step for all running sequences (with chunked prefill so long prompts do not stall others), and retire finished ones immediately. Manage KV cache blocks with paging, support preemption when memory is short, and prioritise to meet latency objectives.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What is chunked prefill, and why does it improve tail latency under mixed traffic?
items.answer: Chunked prefill splits long prompt processing into smaller pieces interleaved with decode steps of other requests. Without it a long prompt monopolises the GPU, stalling everyone's token generation. Interleaving keeps inter-token latency steady, at some cost to the long request's time to first token.
keyPoints: Slower first token for the long request

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Your edit model's output is a full 500-line file. Applying it verbatim is slow and error-prone. How do you make applying edits fast and reliable?
items.answer: Have the model output a diff or targeted edit blocks instead of the whole file, apply them with deterministic matching, and use a small specialised model or algorithm to merge when matching fails. Verify by parsing and running linters or tests, and fall back to full rewrite or asking for a retry if verification fails.
keyPoints: Diffs or edit blocks, not full files

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: After a foundation-model version upgrade, your production agent's escalation rate doubles overnight. Walk through your response.
items.answer: First stabilise: roll back or pin the previous model version if impact is severe. Then compare traces before and after for changes in tool use, refusals or formatting, run your eval suite on both versions, and find the regressed behaviours. Adjust prompts or schemas, add the failures to the evals, and require passing them before the next upgrade.
keyPoints: Compare traces and run evals on both

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: An agent you shipped four months ago runs on a base model that is being deprecated in 60 days. How do you swap models without regressing quality, and what had to be in place beforehand?
items.answer: Needed beforehand: a versioned eval suite, prompts under version control, traces to find real usage, and an abstraction over the model. Run the suite on candidate models, tune prompts, canary traffic with monitoring, and keep the ability to roll back. Start early because quality and behaviour differences take iteration.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design an end-to-end pipeline producing preference data for a frontier lab: 100,000 comparisons a week with quality guarantees.
items.answer: Generate prompts and candidate responses, route comparison tasks to trained annotators through a queue, include gold items and redundancy, track agreement and per-annotator accuracy, adjudicate disagreements, and run automated checks for fraud such as pasted model output. Monitor throughput and quality dashboards and deliver in versioned batches with audits.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What observability does a production LLM system need?
items.answer: Traces for each request showing prompts, retrieved context, tool calls and outputs; metrics for latency, tokens, cost and errors; quality signals from evals and user feedback; and versions of prompts and models on each trace. Dashboards and alerts on rates and percentiles, with privacy controls on logged data.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: A customer says 'the model got worse' after you upgraded the model version in their deployment. How do you verify and respond?
items.answer: Ask for examples, then reproduce by running the same inputs on both versions. Compare against their acceptance criteria with an eval set, separate real regressions from prompt sensitivity or sampling noise, and tune prompts or settings if needed. Offer to pin the old version while fixing, and share findings transparently.
keyPoints: Run both versions on an eval set

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design a customer-support agent that can take real actions, with escalation to humans.
items.answer: Understand intent, retrieve policy and account data, and call scoped tools (look up order, issue refund within limits, update address) with backend-enforced rules. Keep conversation state, confirm actions with the customer, and escalate on low confidence, sensitive topics or policy limits with a summary. Evaluate on simulated and historical conversations, and monitor resolution, escalation and customer satisfaction.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design a code assistant: repository indexing, context assembly, edit application and evaluation.
items.answer: Index code with syntax-aware chunks, embeddings and a symbol graph, kept fresh incrementally. For each request assemble context from the open file, retrieved relevant code, and recent edits, within a token budget. Apply edits as diffs, verify with the language server and tests, and evaluate offline on benchmark tasks and online with acceptance rates and retention.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design an answer engine: a user types a question and gets a cited, streamed answer within a three-second budget.
items.answer: Rewrite the query, run parallel retrieval from web search and caches, rerank and dedupe, assemble the best passages, and stream a generation with inline citations. Use small fast models for rewriting and reranking, cache popular queries, and start streaming as soon as evidence is ready. Verify citations and track latency by stage.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design the harmful-content detection system for uploads on a large social platform.
items.answer: Combine hash matching for known content, classifiers for images, video, text and audio, and LLMs for context-dependent policy decisions. Score and route: auto-action for high confidence, human review for borderline, and appeals. Handle scale with staged models, monitor precision and recall by category and region, and keep adapting to adversarial behaviour.
keyPoints: Hash matching plus classifiers plus LLMs

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design the recommendation system for a short-video feed.
items.answer: Two stages: candidate generation (collaborative and content-based retrieval from embeddings) followed by ranking with a model predicting engagement and quality signals, then a re-ranker for diversity and policy. Use real-time features, handle cold start, evaluate offline with ranking metrics and online with A/B tests, and watch for feedback loops.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: You ship notification summarisation to hundreds of millions of users in 30+ locales and cannot log user content. Design the evaluation and regression-detection story.
items.answer: Evaluate offline on synthetic and consented human-written data in each locale with automated and human grading. Online, use privacy-preserving signals such as aggregated opt-outs, user toggles and on-device feedback counts, differential privacy for statistics, and staged rollouts with guardrail metrics. Maintain per-locale test suites and gate releases on them.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How do you manage prompt versioning and rollbacks in production?
items.answer: Store prompts in version control or a registry with identifiers, link each deployed version to eval results, and have the application fetch a labelled version (staging, production). Roll back by moving the label, and record the prompt version on every trace so regressions can be traced to a change.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Your agent passes 92% of eval tasks. Why might that number be misleading, and what would you measure instead?
items.answer: The tasks may not reflect real traffic, the set may be too easy or leaked, failures may cluster in important slices, and a single run hides variance. Also check what the 8% are, how costly they are, and whether safety-critical cases are covered. Measure per-slice success over repeated runs, severity-weighted errors and production outcomes.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Write the server-side handler for streaming token generation and handle client disconnects correctly.
items.answer: Return a streaming response from an async generator that yields tokens as they arrive from the model. Detect disconnects by checking whether the client is still connected or catching cancellation, and then cancel the upstream generation to stop spending GPU time. Add timeouts, backpressure handling and cleanup in a finally block.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Write a service that proxies streaming text-to-speech to a browser and cancels cleanly when the user navigates away.
items.answer: Open the upstream stream and forward audio chunks to the client as they arrive. When the client connection closes, cancel the upstream request immediately so no more audio is generated or billed. Use backpressure, per-chunk timeouts, and tests that simulate disconnects.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How would you ensure a chatbot intent returns the correct answer, and what precautions would you take before deploying it?
items.answer: Write test conversations for each intent including paraphrases and edge cases, measure intent accuracy and answer correctness, and add fallback behaviour for low-confidence inputs. Review with domain experts, run in staging, monitor after launch, and keep a feedback loop to retrain or fix intents.

source.title: Accenture LLM Operations Engineer interview experience (GeeksforGeeks)

items.question: How do you manage cloud costs for an LLM application?
items.answer: Tag and attribute spend, set budgets and alerts, right-size infrastructure, use autoscaling and spot or reserved capacity where suitable, and reduce model costs with caching, routing to smaller models and prompt trimming. Review usage regularly and track cost per request or per successful task.

source.title: Accenture LLM Operations Engineer interview experience (GeeksforGeeks)

items.question: A customer insists on fine-tuning an open model on their support tickets because they want their own model, but you think retrieval solves it. What do you do?
items.answer: Understand their goal (tone, accuracy, ownership, cost), then run a quick comparison: a retrieval and prompting baseline versus a small fine-tune on held-out tickets. Show the evidence, explain the maintenance costs of fine-tuning, and agree on criteria. If retrieval meets the goal, ship it; fine-tune later if gaps remain.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: A customer indexed ten times more documents and says answer quality got noticeably worse. Drive the investigation.
items.answer: Check whether retrieval degraded (recall dropped, more near-duplicates, noisier top results), whether index settings such as ANN parameters no longer suit the size, whether new content changed the distribution, and whether the prompt now receives more conflicting context. Re-run the eval set on the old and new index, then adjust chunking, filters, reranking or index parameters.
keyPoints: Compare retrieval metrics before and after

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: An enterprise customer reports that responses from your deployed system have become slow. Walk through the diagnosis.
items.answer: Check dashboards and traces for which stage slowed: queueing, retrieval, prompt length, model latency or network. Compare with recent deploys, traffic changes and provider status, look at p95 and p99, and test their specific requests. Mitigate (scale, route to a faster model, roll back), then write up the cause and prevention.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: A customer executive says 'the AI keeps getting things wrong' and wants to cancel the pilot. Walk through your next 48 hours.
items.answer: Listen first, collect concrete failing examples, and acknowledge the problem. Triage the failures into causes (data, retrieval, prompt, scope), fix quick wins, and set up a small eval set from their examples so progress is measurable. Share a plan with metrics and dates, agree on the success criteria, and show improvement quickly.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: An enterprise customer says their assistant hallucinates too much in a RAG-based knowledge tool. What happens in the first 48 hours?
items.answer: Collect examples and classify each failure: missing documents, bad retrieval, ignored context or unsupported claims. Add quick mitigations (abstain when evidence is weak, require citations, tighten prompts), measure faithfulness and retrieval recall on a small labelled set, and propose a plan with metrics. Communicate findings and next steps clearly.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: A customer's LLM chatbot on 8 GPUs is 'too slow and too expensive'. You have one week with them. What do you do?
items.answer: Day one: profile traffic, prompt and output lengths, GPU utilisation and latency breakdown. Likely wins: continuous batching with a modern serving engine, prefix caching, quantisation, prompt trimming, routing easy queries to a smaller model, and right-sizing the cluster. Apply the biggest wins first, validate quality with evals, and leave them with dashboards.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design an on-prem deployment of an open-weight model for a European bank that cannot send data to any external API.
items.answer: Deploy inside the bank's network on dedicated GPUs with a serving engine such as vLLM behind an internal gateway, with identity integration, audit logging and encryption. Pick a model and quantisation that fits the hardware, keep retrieval data on-prem, and plan updates, monitoring and capacity. Validate quality with the bank's own evals and document compliance controls.
keyPoints: Dedicated on-prem GPUs and serving engine

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: A bank wants the whole stack (model, RAG, agents) deployed air-gapped on its own GPUs. What actually changes versus your SaaS?
items.answer: No outbound calls, so models, embeddings, rerankers and dependencies are delivered as artifacts and updated through controlled releases. Monitoring and logging stay inside the perimeter, capacity planning moves to the customer, and support is harder, so you need good diagnostics and documentation. Security reviews and change management become part of the delivery.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: A customer's managed-platform workload costs too much. Cut inference cost dramatically without unacceptable quality loss.
items.answer: Measure what drives spend (tokens per request, model choice, request volume), then trim prompts, cache, route simple requests to cheaper models, batch offline workloads, and consider provisioned throughput if volume is steady. Re-run evals after each change to confirm quality holds.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design a multi-tenant inference platform that serves many foundation models to thousands of customers.
items.answer: A control plane for model catalogue, access and quotas, and a data plane of inference fleets per model with autoscaling. Isolate tenants with identity, per-tenant quotas, encryption and no cross-tenant caching, and meter usage for billing. Support regions, versioning, safety filters and noisy-neighbour protection.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Price a dedicated endpoint: estimate cost per million output tokens for a 70B model and explain the throughput-latency trade.
items.answer: Cost per million tokens is GPU cost per hour divided by tokens generated per hour, divided into millions. Throughput depends on batch size: bigger batches raise tokens per second per GPU but increase each user's latency. So choose a batch size that meets the latency target, compute the throughput, and then derive cost, adjusting for utilisation.
keyPoints: Cost = GPU hourly cost / tokens per hour

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Can a 70B-parameter model be served on a single 80 GB GPU? Walk through whether it fits and what throughput to expect.
items.answer: FP16 weights alone are about 140 GB, so no. At 8-bit they are 70 GB, leaving little room for KV cache; at 4-bit about 35 GB, which fits with room for cache. Single-stream speed is bandwidth-bound, around memory bandwidth divided by weight bytes, so roughly 50 to 100 tokens per second depending on quantisation, lower in practice.
keyPoints: FP16 is 140 GB, does not fit
Decode speed is bandwidth / weight bytes

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: When would you choose vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM or a custom serving stack?
items.answer: vLLM is a flexible, widely used default with paged attention and broad model support. SGLang is strong for structured and multi-call programs with prefix reuse. TensorRT-LLM gives maximum speed on NVIDIA hardware at the cost of more build and tuning effort. A custom stack is justified only for unusual hardware or requirements. Benchmark on your own workload.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Why was safetensors created when pickle-based checkpoints already worked everywhere?
items.answer: Pickle can execute arbitrary code when loaded, so a malicious checkpoint can compromise the machine. Safetensors stores tensors in a simple format without code execution, and supports fast zero-copy and lazy loading. It is safer and often faster to load.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: A customer wants to migrate from a proprietary frontier-model API to an open model. How do you run that engagement?
items.answer: Define success criteria and build an evaluation set from their real traffic. Benchmark candidate open models, tune prompts, estimate cost and hosting needs, then pilot on a slice of traffic with fallback to the old API. Compare quality, latency and cost, and migrate gradually while keeping the ability to roll back.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: If a customer wanted to leave one observability platform and move to an open-source alternative, what would you do?
items.answer: Understand why they want to move (cost, control, features), inventory what they use (traces, evals, datasets, dashboards), and map each to the alternative. Export data, run both in parallel for a period, validate parity, and plan the cutover. Be honest about gaps and offer ways to bridge them.

source.title: LangChain FDE interview experience (Exponent)

items.question: How do vision-language models get images into an LLM: projector, cross-attention or native tokens?
items.answer: A vision encoder splits the image into patches and produces embeddings. A projector (a small MLP) maps them into the LLM's embedding space as extra tokens, which is the simplest approach; cross-attention layers let the LLM attend to image features without lengthening the sequence; natively multimodal models are trained from the start on interleaved image and text tokens. Trade-offs involve token count, training cost and quality.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Why use a native dynamic-resolution vision encoder instead of fixed tiling, and what does multimodal rotary position encode?
items.answer: Native resolution keeps the image's aspect ratio and detail, avoiding distortion from resizing or awkward tile boundaries, and adjusts token count to image size. Multimodal rotary embeddings encode positions along several axes (height, width, and time for video) so the model knows where each patch sits spatially and temporally.
keyPoints: Positions along height, width and time

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What changes when you move from understanding images to understanding video?
items.answer: Video adds time: many frames mean far more tokens, so you sample frames, compress tokens (pooling, merging) or use temporal encoders. The model needs temporal position information and must reason about motion and events, and evaluation needs video-specific benchmarks. Audio often matters too.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design a document-intelligence pipeline: scanned PDFs in, structured fields out, at 10 million documents.
items.answer: Classify document types, run OCR or a vision model for layout and text, extract fields against a schema, and validate with rules and cross-field checks. Route low-confidence results to human review, store provenance for each field (page and region), and process in queues with retries. Track accuracy per field and document type and improve from corrections.
keyPoints: Classify, OCR or vision, schema extraction

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Clinicians will not sign what they cannot verify. How would you build span-level provenance from every line of the clinical note back to the conversation?
items.answer: Generate the note in structured form where each statement carries references to the transcript segments (with timestamps) that support it. Verify with an alignment or entailment check, show the evidence on hover in the UI, and flag statements without support. Measure the share of statements with valid support.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: A generated clinical note contains a medication the patient never mentioned. Treat that as a safety incident: how do you detect it before a clinician sees it?
items.answer: Verify extracted entities such as medications against the transcript with grounded checks, and flag any entity without supporting text. Cross-check against the patient's chart for plausibility without letting the chart introduce unsupported claims, block or highlight flagged items, and log incidents for review. Track these rates and treat each as a regression test.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How do you handle code-switching and accents in a production speech recognition system?
items.answer: Collect and train on real code-mixed and accented data, use language-agnostic or multilingual models, add domain vocabulary biasing, and evaluate with word error rate sliced by accent and language mix. Post-process with a language model for normalisation, and keep a feedback loop from corrections.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design a diarisation system that attributes speaker roles, such as doctor versus patient, and not just anonymous clusters.
items.answer: Cluster speaker embeddings to separate voices, then assign roles using cues like who asks questions, vocabulary, enrolment of the clinician's voice and conversation structure. Combine acoustic and text-based models, handle overlap and noisy rooms, and measure diarisation error rate and role accuracy.
keyPoints: Role cues from text and enrolment

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How do you evaluate speech recognition beyond word error rate, and speech synthesis when there is no single correct output?
items.answer: For recognition, look at error types on important words (names, numbers, medical terms), slice by accent and noise, and measure downstream task success. For synthesis, use human listening tests (mean opinion score, preference comparisons), intelligibility measured via recognition, speaker similarity and pronunciation checks on tricky text.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Text normalisation is where speech synthesis quality often breaks in production. Walk through it, including code-mixed text.
items.answer: Convert numbers, dates, currencies, abbreviations and symbols into spoken words according to language and context, handle mixed scripts and transliteration, and apply pronunciation dictionaries for names and brands. Prosody depends on correct phrasing, so punctuation and sentence splitting matter. Test with tricky inputs and collect listener reports.
keyPoints: Context-aware expansion of numbers and dates

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Budget the latency for a real-time voice agent: voice activity detection, recognition, the LLM, synthesis and the network. Where does the time go?
items.answer: Target around 800 ms to 1 s response. End-of-speech detection can take 200 to 500 ms, streaming recognition adds little after speech ends, the LLM's first token is often 200 to 400 ms, synthesis time to first audio 100 to 300 ms, and the network adds 50 to 150 ms. Overlap stages by streaming and starting synthesis on partial output, and choose models for speed.
keyPoints: LLM first token and TTS first audio

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Cascaded recognition, LLM and synthesis versus native speech-to-speech models: argue both sides.
items.answer: Cascaded systems are modular, easy to debug, let you pick best-of-breed components and insert tools and guardrails on text, but add latency and lose tone and emotion. Speech-to-speech models respond faster, preserve prosody and handle interruptions naturally, but are harder to control, evaluate and ground with tools. Many products start cascaded and move to hybrids.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design barge-in and interruption handling for a voice agent.
items.answer: Run voice activity detection on the user's microphone while the agent speaks. On detected speech, stop playback quickly, cancel in-flight generation and synthesis, and tell the model what was actually spoken so its state matches. Filter echo and background noise to avoid false interruptions, and treat short backchannels such as 'uh-huh' separately.
keyPoints: Update state with what was spoken

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design a real-time voice agent for a citizen helpline in Hindi and three regional languages, targeting under 250 ms perceived latency over a phone line.
items.answer: Perceived latency of 250 ms is very tight, so use streaming recognition with fast endpointing, a small fast model (or speech-to-speech) hosted close to the telephony provider, immediate acknowledgements or filler to cover compute time, and streaming synthesis. Handle telephone-quality audio, language identification, code-mixing and fallbacks to humans. Measure latency end to end per language.
keyPoints: Small model near the telephony edge
Phone-quality audio, language ID, human fallback

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: A contact centre wants to replace its IVR with voice agents. Run the engagement.
items.answer: Map current call flows and volumes, choose a few high-volume intents to automate first, and build with escalation to humans. Create evaluation call sets, measure containment, transfer rate, accuracy and customer satisfaction, and pilot on a share of traffic. Handle integrations, compliance and recording consent, and expand after meeting targets.
keyPoints: Map flows and pick starting intents

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How would you build multimodal retrieval over images, video and text in one index?
items.answer: Use a joint embedding model that maps images and text into a shared space, or caption and transcribe media to text and index that too, often both. Store metadata, chunk video by scenes, and query with text or images. Rerank with a multimodal model and evaluate on a labelled cross-modal set.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: You need to run a roughly 3B-parameter language model on a phone with tight memory and power budgets. What changes versus a datacentre?
items.answer: Quantise weights to 4 bits or lower with quantisation-aware training where needed, use grouped-query attention and compact KV caches, limit context, and use the neural engine or GPU efficiently. Memory, thermal and battery limits dominate, so optimise time to first token and sustained throughput, and share one base model across features with small adapters.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Explain post-training quantisation versus quantisation-aware training. What breaks at 2 to 4 bits, and how do you recover quality?
items.answer: Post-training quantisation converts trained weights to lower precision using calibration data, quick but can lose accuracy. Quantisation-aware training simulates low precision during training so the model adapts. At 2 to 4 bits, outlier weights and activations hurt; remedies include group-wise scales, outlier handling, mixed precision for sensitive layers, and fine-tuning or adapters to recover accuracy.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Give your decision framework for prompting versus RAG versus fine-tuning, with cost and latency attached.
items.answer: Start with prompting (cheapest, fastest to iterate). Add RAG when the model lacks knowledge or the knowledge changes. Fine-tune when you need consistent style, format or behaviour, lower latency or cost through a smaller model, or capabilities prompting cannot reach, and you have quality data. Decide with evals, and note fine-tuning's costs: data work, training, hosting and maintenance.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: When would you fine-tune instead of using RAG or prompting, and if you do, LoRA or full fine-tuning?
items.answer: Fine-tune when you need reliable format or tone, domain-specific behaviour, or to distil a larger model into a cheaper one, and prompting plus RAG fall short. Default to LoRA or QLoRA: far less memory, quick to train, adapters are easy to swap. Choose full fine-tuning only with lots of data, big behaviour change and the budget to match.
keyPoints: Behaviour, format and cost use cases

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: After fine-tuning on a customer's task, target accuracy is up but the model got worse at everything else. What happened and what do you do?
items.answer: That is catastrophic forgetting: updates for the new task overwrote general abilities. Reduce the learning rate and epochs, use LoRA with low rank so the base weights are preserved, mix in general instruction data, regularise, and evaluate on regression sets outside the task. If the narrow task is all you need, accept it; otherwise use adapters you can toggle.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Do the GPU memory maths for full fine-tuning a 7B model in bf16 with Adam. Now with LoRA.
items.answer: Full fine-tuning: weights 14 GB (bf16), gradients 14 GB, Adam states usually fp32 (8 bytes per parameter, 56 GB) plus often a master copy, so roughly 90 to 100 GB before activations. LoRA freezes the base weights (14 GB) and trains small adapters whose gradients and optimizer states are tiny, so a few gigabytes plus activations; QLoRA with a 4-bit base brings the base to about 4 GB.
keyPoints: Weights 14 GB + grads 14 GB + Adam 56 GB
LoRA: frozen base, tiny trainable state

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Explain the LoRA decomposition. Why does it work, and how do you choose the rank?
items.answer: LoRA freezes a weight matrix W and learns an update as the product of two small matrices B and A with rank r, so the effective weight is W plus BA scaled by alpha over r. It works because fine-tuning updates tend to have low intrinsic rank. Choose r by trying a few values (like 8, 16, 64) on your eval set; higher rank adds capacity and cost, with diminishing returns.
keyPoints: W + BA with low rank r

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Fine-tune an 8B model on a single 24 GB GPU. Walk through the memory maths and the stack you would use.
items.answer: Load the base in 4-bit (about 5 GB), train LoRA adapters with a paged optimizer, enable gradient checkpointing, use a small micro-batch with gradient accumulation and short sequences. Memory then fits within 24 GB. Use a library stack such as transformers, PEFT, bitsandbytes and TRL, and evaluate against the unquantised baseline.
keyPoints: PEFT, bitsandbytes, TRL; compare to baseline

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What is DPO and why did it displace PPO-based RLHF at many labs? When is online RL still better?
items.answer: Direct preference optimisation trains directly on preference pairs with a classification-style loss against a reference model, with no separate reward model or RL loop, so it is simpler and more stable. Online RL still helps when you have a reliable reward signal or verifier and want the model to explore beyond the data, as in reasoning and agentic tasks.
keyPoints: Preference pairs, no reward model or RL loop
Online RL for exploration with verifiable rewards

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Explain Constitutional AI. What does it buy you over vanilla RLHF, and what does it not solve?
items.answer: Constitutional AI uses a written set of principles so the model critiques and revises its own outputs, and AI feedback (RLAIF) trained on those principles replaces much of the human labelling. It makes values more explicit and scalable and reduces the need for humans to see harmful content. It does not guarantee the principles are right or complete, and it does not remove the need for evaluation and oversight.
keyPoints: Principles guide self-critique and AI feedback
Reduces human exposure to harmful data
Does not guarantee correctness; still needs evals

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: We sell reinforcement-learning environments. Design one for 'book a multi-city trip in a web travel app', specify the reward, and say how you stop the policy hacking it.
items.answer: Build a simulated travel site with deterministic state and realistic failures. Reward verifiable outcomes: the final booking satisfies constraints (cities, dates, budget), with partial credit for sub-goals and penalties for invalid actions. Prevent hacking by checking final state rather than claims, hiding some checks, randomising layouts, and monitoring rollouts for exploits.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, and where does it beat a learned reward model?
items.answer: RLVR trains with rewards computed by programmatic checks, such as unit tests passing or a maths answer matching, instead of a model of human preference. It beats a learned reward model on tasks with checkable answers because the reward is precise and hard to game, though it does not apply to open-ended quality judgements.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What is distillation, and how do you build a strong small model from a large one?
items.answer: Use a strong teacher to generate outputs (or soft labels), filter them for quality, and train the student on them with supervised learning or logit matching. Choose diverse prompts, verify answers where possible, and evaluate the student against the teacher on your tasks. Check the teacher's terms of use.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: You have one on-device base model but a dozen features such as summarising, rewriting and reply suggestions. How do you specialise without shipping a dozen models?
items.answer: Train small task-specific adapters (LoRA) on the shared base and load or swap them at runtime, so only the adapter weights differ per feature. Share the quantised base in memory, evaluate each adapter against the base on its task, and manage versions so they stay compatible with the base.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: What problem do chat templates solve, and what goes wrong when they are ignored?
items.answer: Chat models are trained with a specific format of special tokens for roles and turns. A chat template renders messages into exactly that format. If you ignore it, the model sees an unfamiliar format and quality drops: it may ignore instructions, ramble or fail to stop, and fine-tuning with the wrong template teaches the wrong format.
keyPoints: Use the same template for tuning and serving

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Tell me about a time you worked on a GenAI project.
items.answer: Pick a project you can discuss in depth. State the problem and users, your role, the architecture and why, a hard technical problem you solved, how you measured quality, and the outcome. Be ready for follow-ups on trade-offs and failures.
keyPoints: A hard problem and how you measured

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: Walk me through your most recent AI engineering work.
items.answer: Explain the goal, the system design, your contribution, the toughest problem and how you evaluated and monitored it in production. Give numbers for scale, quality and cost where possible, and say what you would change.

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: Present a past AI-focused solution that you worked on.
items.answer: Structure it as problem, constraints, approach, results, and lessons. Use a diagram, quantify impact, explain trade-offs and alternatives rejected, and be candid about what did not work. Keep to the time limit and leave room for questions.

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: Why do you want to join an AI-first company, and why us in particular?
items.answer: Connect your motivation to specifics: the mission, products and technical problems of that company, and how your experience fits. Show that you have used and thought critically about their products, and be honest about where you disagree or what concerns you.

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: Where do you think AI is headed, and where could it go wrong?
items.answer: Give a grounded view: likely progress in capabilities and agents, the practical limits, and concrete risks such as misuse, errors in high-stakes use, concentration of power and security. Describe what engineers can do, such as evaluation, safeguards and transparency, rather than only predicting.

source.title: OpenAI software engineer interview guide (Aced, formerly Exponent)

items.question: Design an enterprise RAG assistant over 10 million documents with per-user permissions.
items.answer: Connectors ingest documents and ACLs; a pipeline parses, chunks and embeds them into hybrid indexes with permission metadata, updated incrementally. At query time filter by the user's permissions, retrieve and rerank, generate with citations, and cache safely. Monitor quality, latency and freshness, and run evals with enterprise-specific questions.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: An agent has started looping on an expensive tool. How do you stop it now and prevent it later?
items.answer: Immediately cap or kill runs and add budgets for steps, tokens and cost. Investigate traces for why it repeats (ambiguous tool results, no progress check) and add repetition detection, clearer tool outputs, and escalation to humans. Add the case to your evals.

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: Why is RAG the right choice for an enterprise assistant rather than fine-tuning on company data, and where does RAG break?
items.answer: RAG keeps answers current, respects per-user permissions and provides citations, while fine-tuned weights go stale and cannot enforce access. It breaks on aggregation questions, multi-hop reasoning, poor source quality and missing retrieval. Fine-tuning is better for style or behaviour, not for knowledge.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How would you evaluate answer quality for an answer engine continuously and at scale, with both automated and human signals?
items.answer: Sample production queries, score with calibrated LLM judges for relevance, faithfulness and citation support, and send a subset to human raters to calibrate and catch judge drift. Combine with online signals such as follow-up queries and feedback, track by query category, and alert on regressions.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: How would you evaluate a meeting-summarisation feature before shipping it to a hundred million users?
items.answer: Build an evaluation set of diverse meetings with expert reference summaries or rubrics, measure coverage, accuracy of action items and decisions, faithfulness and tone, and compare models and prompts. Test edge cases such as noisy audio and multiple languages, run a staged rollout with user feedback and guardrail metrics, and review privacy.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Walk through how you would integrate a foundation model into a customer's existing production pipeline.
items.answer: Understand the pipeline, data flows and constraints, find where the model adds value, and prototype a thin integration with fallbacks. Add evaluation on real data, handle security, latency and cost, roll out gradually behind a flag, and monitor. Document trade-offs and ownership.

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: A GenAI product has had a year of investment and no traction. Do you continue or kill it?
items.answer: Diagnose why: wrong problem, wrong users, poor quality, poor distribution or too early. Look at usage, retention, qualitative feedback and unit economics, define what evidence would justify continuing, and run a short time-boxed experiment. Decide on data and be willing to stop.

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: How would you build a reliable workflow for a long-running task that risks timing out?
items.answer: Break the task into resumable steps with checkpoints stored outside the model, run it as a background job with a queue, and make steps idempotent so retries are safe. Stream progress, set per-step timeouts, and persist intermediate results so a failure resumes rather than restarts. Notify the user on completion.

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: How do you stay up to date with developments in AI?
items.answer: Describe a routine: a few trusted sources (papers, release notes, newsletters, practitioner blogs), hands-on testing of new models against your own eval set, and discussion with peers. Show you separate real capability changes from hype by testing, and give an example of something you adopted or rejected after trying it.
keyPoints: Test new models on your own evals

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: A new frontier model is released and scores better on your benchmarks. What happens before it reaches customers?
items.answer: Run the full eval suite on real-task data, compare with the current model per slice, and look at failures and regressions that averages hide. Check latency, cost, safety behaviour and format changes, tune prompts, get expert review on important workflows, then roll out gradually with monitoring and the ability to revert.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Which framework did you use in your project and why? How do you ensure the quality of the output?
items.answer: Justify the framework by the needs it met (orchestration, tools, ecosystem) and what you traded away. For quality, describe your evaluation set, automated checks, human review, guardrails and monitoring, and give a number if you can.

source.title: Accenture LLM Operations Engineer interview experience (GeeksforGeeks)

items.question: Tell me about a technical misjudgement that delayed a project.
items.answer: Use a real example: the decision, why it seemed reasonable, how you found out it was wrong, what it cost, and what you changed in your process afterwards. Take ownership without blaming others.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Design an ML system for fraud identification, with heavy class imbalance and an adversarial opponent.
items.answer: Use real-time features and rules plus a model trained with class-imbalance techniques and appropriate metrics (precision-recall, cost-weighted), with human review for borderline cases. Expect adversaries to adapt, so monitor drift, retrain frequently, use graph signals, and keep feedback loops from confirmed fraud. Balance false positives against customer friction.

source.title: Aced (formerly Exponent) interview question bank

items.question: Describe a time you had a conflict with a coworker or stakeholder, and a time you disagreed with your manager.
items.answer: Use a clear structure: situation, what each side wanted, what you did to understand and resolve it, the outcome and what you learned. Show respect, data-driven reasoning and willingness to commit once a decision is made.

source.title: OpenAI software engineer interview guide (Aced, formerly Exponent)

items.question: How would you make complex AI research findings accessible to a non-technical audience?
items.answer: Start with why it matters, use plain language and analogies, show one concrete example, state the limits honestly, and avoid jargon unless defined. Check understanding with questions and tailor depth to the audience.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Your conversational agent will face effectively infinite possible conversations. How do you evaluate it before launch?
items.answer: Build a scenario library from real or expected conversations, use simulated users to cover variety, define success criteria (task completion, policy adherence, tone), and grade with a mix of automated checks and human review. Include adversarial and edge cases, run repeatedly for variance, and gate launch on thresholds plus a monitored staged rollout.

source.title: AI Engineering Interview Questions Company Wise (Outcome School, GitHub)

items.question: Tell me about a time you made short-term sacrifices for long-term gains.
items.answer: Choose a story where you accepted a visible cost, such as delaying a feature to fix infrastructure, for a later benefit. Describe the trade-off analysis, how you got buy-in, the result with evidence, and what you learned.
